target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound credential payload reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QA Lab credential add commands enforced `OPENCLAW_QA_CREDENTIAL_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` with a file stat before reading the payload. A payload file could grow after that stat and before the read, which let the command read and parse data beyond the configured cap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The credential payload reader now opens the file, verifies the opened handle is a regular file, and reads at most `maxBytes + 1` bytes from that handle. That keeps boundary-sized payload JSON accepted while rejecting files that are oversized at stat time or grow past the cap before the read, without reading the whole grown file into memory.

## User Impact

Operators using QA Lab credential pools get the configured payload byte limit applied to the actual bytes consumed by the CLI. Oversized or racing payload files fail before any credential broker request is sent.

## Evidence

- Current head: `36c45dbc46e05dd87fb89a21e204d59b27e6850e`.
- Focused formatter proof: `oxfmt --check extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check -- extensions/qa-lab/src/cli.runtime.ts` passed.

## Related independent bug-family PRs

This is an independent bounded-file-read fix for QA Lab credential payloads. It is not stacked on any sibling PR and has no merge dependency.

target.title: feat(gateway): pre-handshake WS verifyClient with Sec-Fetch-Site and forwarded-header hardening
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's gateway validates browser `Origin` on the WebSocket path only **post-handshake** (in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-admission.ts`, after the socket is already open). This leaves gaps the WebSocket upgrade phase is the only reliable place to close:

- **Header-smuggling / contradiction attacks** — a client forging `X-Forwarded-For` to disagree with `Forwarded` (or vice-versa) to confuse the resolved client IP / trust decision.
- **Cross-site WebSocket initiations (CSRF / DNS-rebinding class)** — there is no `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate anywhere in `main`.
- **Proto contradiction** — `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `Forwarded proto` disagreeing with the actual socket transport (without breaking legitimate TLS-terminating trusted proxies).

This PR adds a self-contained **pre-handshake** `verifyClient` gate on the gateway `WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })`, so unauthenticated or forged clients never complete the HTTP 101 upgrade. This is the WebSocket-upgrade sibling of the HTTP ingress CSRF work already on `main` (#102834, #96486) and complements the origin-allowlist work in #98924 (which decides *which* origins pass, not *when/how the gate runs*). The existing post-handshake origin check in `connect-admission.ts` is unchanged and remains authoritative for role-scoped decisions.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Pre-handshake beats post-handshake** — a rejected client never gets a live socket.
- **Reuses the shared `checkBrowserOrigin`** rather than reinventing origin logic.
- **All strictness is opt-in and default-off** (`gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation`, `rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders`, `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests`), so existing deployments have **zero behavior change**. Non-browser clients (CLI, native apps) send no `Origin` and pass through; they authenticate post-handshake as today.
- **Trusted proxies are correctly exempted** from the proto-mismatch check — a TLS-terminating proxy legitimately presents plaintext to the gateway.

## User Impact

- Network-exposed gateways gain a pre-handshake defense against forged forwarded headers and cross-site WebSocket CSRF, with **no config change required** for existing users (all new behavior opt-in).
- Operators who want stricter posture can enable:
  - `gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation` — reject duplicate / comma-chained sensitive proxy headers and proto contradictions.
  - `gateway.security.rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders` — reject proxy headers from non-trusted peers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` — reject `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` / `cross-origin` WebSocket upgrades. **Off by default**; opt in only when every legitimate browser WS client is same-origin to the gateway.

## Evidence

### Current-head live WebSocket Upgrade proof

A real `node:http` server with a real `ws.WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, verifyClient })`, wired through the **production** `createGatewayVerifyClient` from this branch, was sent real HTTP Upgrade requests over a raw socket (the same wire path the production gateway uses — not a mock). Sensitive-header duplicate/chain cases are sent as raw duplicate header lines, because Node's normalized `req.headers` collapses them before handler code runs; `validateSensitiveHeaders` reads `req.rawHeaders` to catch exactly that.

```
== LIVE WS UPGRADE PROOF (head 5924fb1314e) ==

[duplicate x-forwarded-for (two raw lines)] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: x-forwarded-for
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[duplicate Host (raw; Node drops 2nd in req.headers)] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: host
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[comma-chained x-forwarded-for] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: x-forwarded-for
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[native client, no Origin] (default)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

[trusted proxy + proxy headers] (strict ON + trusted)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

[duplicate xff but strict OFF (default)] (no breakage)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

RESULT: ALL CASES PASSED
```

This directly proves the two reviewer asks on the current head:
- **Duplicate sensitive-header rejection** — cases 1–3 show `strictHeaderValidation` rejects duplicate and comma-chained `x-forwarded-for` / `host` at the 101 boundary, reading from `req.rawHeaders` so Node's normalized view can't hide the duplicates.
- **Accepted compatibility case** — case 4 (native client, no Origin) and case 5 (trusted proxy presenting proxy headers under `strictHeaderValidation`) both complete the upgrade; case 6 confirms the default-off posture introduces zero breakage for the existing duplicate-header traffic some proxies emit.

### Full behavior matrix (unit + wire, this branch)

| # | Scenario | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Native client, no Origin | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 2 | Loopback-alias browser (`localhost`→`127.0.0.1`, cross-site) — v2026.4.15 contract | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 3 | Allowed browser Origin (allowlist) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 4 | Disallowed browser Origin | `403 Forbidden` |
| 5 | Cross-site WS rejection (flag opt-in) | `403 Forbidden` |
| 6 | Forwarded-header contradiction (IPv6) | `400 Bad Request` |
| 7 | Forwarded-header agreement (IPv6 bracketed+port vs bracketed) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 8 | Proto mismatch from untrusted peer | `400 Bad Request` |
| 9 | Proto mismatch from trusted proxy (TLS-terminating) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 10 | Untrusted proxy headers (opt-in) | `403 Forbidden` |
| 11 | Literal `null` Origin (opaque context) | `403 Forbidden` |

Tests: `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` (11/11 passing), `tsgo` core typecheck clean, `oxlint`/`oxfmt` clean on touched files.

## Scope

- **In scope:** `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts` (new, wired at `server-runtime-state.ts`), `src/gateway/forwarded-headers.ts` (validators), their tests, and the `gateway.security.*` config surface in `src/config/types.gateway.ts` + `src/config/zod-schema.gateway.ts`.
- **Out of scope:** the `#98924` allowlist-wildcard contract and the broader `gateway.browserOrigins` policy direction.

## Related

- Sibling enforcement: #98924 (`allowedOriginPatterns`).
- Prior art this complements (addressed on `main`): #102834 (HTTP ingress CSRF under `auth.mode=none`), #96486 (CSRF via `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`, reused verbatim here).

target.title: fix(cli): offer config repair after invalid startup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users starting or restarting OpenClaw with a structurally invalid, repairable config received validation errors but no consent-gated path to repair and retry the operation.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI now owns one typed invalid-config recovery flow: interactive terminals offer `openclaw doctor --fix` with a default-yes prompt, run it only after consent, and retry once. Headless runs print the exact command without mutating config. Manual-only Nix and plugin-packaging failures remain blocked, and SecretRef or arbitrary startup failures are unchanged.

## User Impact

Operators can repair known-shape startup config failures in place from an interactive CLI. Automation remains safe: it never runs doctor without consent, and repeated failures stop after one retry.

AI-assisted: yes. The implementation and evidence were reviewed with the repository `autoreview` workflow; final branch review reported no actionable findings.

## Evidence

- Focused Node 24 Vitest run: 126 tests passed across the recovery helper, config guard, typed invalid-config, Gateway startup recovery, and Gateway command suites.
- Blacksmith Testbox exact-head proof: `pnpm tsgo`, `pnpm check:test-types`, `pnpm docs:check-mdx`, touched-file `pnpm format`, touched-file oxlint, `git diff --check`, and `pnpm deadcode:exports` all passed. Run: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29635906152
- Isolated headless live run: invalid config exited 78, printed `openclaw doctor --fix`, did not prompt, and left the config unchanged.
- Isolated tmux live run: default-yes offer launched doctor, repaired an unknown key, retried the foreground Gateway once, reached `gateway ready`, then shut down cleanly via SIGINT. All real LaunchAgent mutation/restart prompts were declined.
- Source-blind behavior validation also confirmed interactive decline prints the command, exits without retry, and leaves config unchanged.

target.title: fix(ollama): strip unconsumed response body on non-OK HTTP responses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`checkOllamaCloudAuth`, `pullOllamaModelCore`, and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` in `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` exit without consuming or cancelling the response body. This affects both non-OK error paths (500, non-401 errors) **and the 200 OK success path** (`/api/me` returning `signedIn: true`). The `release()` callback from `fetchWithSsrFGuard` only calls `cleanup()` and `closeDispatcher()` — it does not cancel `response.body`. Repeated healthy cloud-auth checks accumulate unconsumed body streams on every call.

## Why This Change Was Made

`await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => {})` is added at all four exit points — three non-OK paths and the 200 OK return. This releases undici resources immediately rather than relying on GC finalizers or dispatcher teardown. The `.catch(() => {})` is deliberate — a failed cancel must not mask the original error or change the return shape.

## User Impact

All Ollama cloud-auth HTTP responses (success and error) now properly release body stream resources. No resource leaks from repeated `/api/me` health checks.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (loopback server)

The proof uses a continuous chunked body stream (interval-based writes every 1ms) to prevent undici from buffering the entire response. Without the fix, the body stream stays open indefinitely. With the fix, `body?.cancel()` closes the connection within single-digit milliseconds.

```
$ node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  ok: response body stream is cancelled
  info: bytes_written_before_cancel=2048 elapsed_ms=239
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 4 passed, 0 failed
```

### Mutation check

Revert all 4 `response.body?.cancel()` lines → body is NOT cancelled on success path:

```
$ git stash && node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  FAIL: response body stream is cancelled
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 3 passed, 1 failed
```

Restore fix → 4/4 passed.

### Vitest (39/39 pass)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  39 passed (39)
```

New: `cancels the response body on successful 200 cloud-auth response` — streaming 200 body with cancel spy.

### Format check

```
$ oxfmt --check extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.
```

### Not tested

- Live Ollama cloud auth API roundtrip with real credentials
- `pullOllamaModelCore` and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` paths (same body-cancel pattern applied)
- `release()` integration with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` dispatcher lifecycle

Resolves a problem where the canonical Matrix maturity lane reported 10 intermittent or harness-caused failures, leaving Matrix at 72/82 despite the covered behavior working.

target.title: fix(codex): stop stale MCP child processes with revalidated SIGKILL escalation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts:1146` sends `process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM")` and immediately records the pid as killed — without verifying the process actually terminated. If a child process traps or ignores SIGTERM (e.g. `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` without `process.exit()`), it survives and becomes a zombie that the periodic health monitor can never clear.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix schedules a SIGKILL after a 2-second grace period. Before sending SIGKILL, it **revalidates process identity**: re-lists processes via `/bin/ps`, finds the PID, and confirms the command still matches a scoped `SkyComputerUseClient` MCP child descendant of the original ancestor PID. This prevents accidental termination of an unrelated process in the rare case of PID reuse during the grace period.

The timer is `unref()`'d so it does not keep the event loop alive. The kill path is macOS-gated (`process.platform !== "darwin"` early return) — no change to the platform guard.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren`, `SIGKILL`, `SIGTERM`, `computer-use`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Codex app-server health monitor now reliably terminates stale Computer Use MCP child processes, even those that ignore SIGTERM. PID reuse is guarded by identity revalidation before escalation. No change for macOS where SIGKILL is already used.

## Evidence

Exact head: `25260529a0e2ac2d491b7ae4f0b8eb08ad114390`

`oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.

### Tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  36 passed (36)
   Start at  16:27:44
   Duration  52.38s
```

New tests cover:
- SIGTERM is sent to identified stale MCP children
- After 2s grace period, revalidation ps confirms identity → SIGKILL is sent
- After 2s, quick existence check (`kill 0`) throws ESRCH → SIGKILL skipped
- After 2s, revalidation ps shows different command → SIGKILL skipped (PID reuse guard)

### Real behavior proof

A standalone proof script exercises the same process lifecycle on a real OS (Linux, Node 24):

```
Ancestor PID (this script): 1555975
Child PID: 1556026
ps revalidation: pid=1556026 ppid=1555975
    command: /usr/local/node/bin/node -e process.on('SIGTERM', ...)
    descendant of 1555975: YES (PASS)
Sent SIGTERM to child 1556026
After SIGTERM: child alive = true (expect true)         ← child traps SIGTERM
Waiting 2s grace period...
Revalidation: pid=1556026 exists, command marker: true  ← identity confirmed
Sent SIGKILL to child 1556026
After SIGKILL: child alive = false (expect false)       ← SIGKILL succeeds
ps after SIGKILL: pid 1556026 in list = false (expect false)

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 1 passed, 0 failed
```

What this proves:
1. **SIGTERM trap**: A child that ignores SIGTERM survives the initial kill
2. **Grace period**: The 2-second delay allows the process to exit gracefully if it can
3. **ps revalidation**: `/bin/ps` process listing correctly identifies the PID, command, and parent-child relationship
4. **SIGKILL escalation**: After revalidation passes, SIGKILL reliably terminates the child
5. **Cleanup confirmation**: Post-SIGKILL ps listing confirms the PID is gone

The only macOS-specific difference is the ps flag format (`-axo` vs `-eo`), which is a simple argument change — the revalidation and kill logic is identical across platforms. The macOS ps format is exercised by the existing `parsePsOutput` unit tests.

### Mutation checks

- Revert the SIGKILL escalation (`git checkout origin/main -- extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts`) → test "revalidates process identity and sends SIGKILL" FAILS: `expected "kill" to be called with arguments: [ 1234, 'SIGKILL' ]`, received 1st call: `[ 1234, 'SIGTERM' ]` (no SIGKILL after timer). Restore fix → 36/36 passed.

### Not tested

- macOS live process lifecycle (SIGTERM→SIGKILL on Darwin; current behavior already uses SIGKILL directly)
- Real Codex MCP child processes in a running app-server
- PID reuse race condition in production (tested via unit tests with timer mocking)

target.title: fix: bound miscellaneous unbounded file reads across 5 modules
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Five modules in the codebase use unbounded fs.readFileSync or fs.promises.readFile calls on user-controlled file paths. A corrupted, malicious, or accidentally enormous file at any of these paths can OOM the process:

1. **src/plugins/bundle-commands.ts** — loadBundleCommandsFromRoot reads plugin bundle command markdown files. Plugin content is user-installed and untrusted.
2. **src/cli/config-set-input.ts** — parseBatchSource reads user-provided CLI batch files.
3. **src/commands/doctor-workspace.ts** — shouldSuggestMemorySystem and migrateLegacyRootMemoryFile read AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md workspace files.
4. **src/trajectory/cleanup.ts** — readTrajectoryPointerFile reads session trajectory pointer JSON files.
5. **src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts** — readConfigExport reads the user config file for diagnostic bundles.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 (https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101472) established readRegularFileSync/readRegularFile from src/infra/regular-file.js with a maxBytes parameter as the standard bounded-read primitive. These five sites were the remaining unbounded synchronous and async fs.readFile calls on user-controlled file paths, identified by a systematic grep for unbounded read calls in the codebase.

Each surface gets a module-specific cap derived from expected content size:
| Surface | Expected Size | Cap | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bundle command markdown | <10 KB | 1 MB | Generous for plugin command files |
| CLI batch file | <100 KB | 8 MB | Supports large batch operations |
| AGENTS.md / MEMORY.md | <500 KB | 10 MB | Very large memory files |
| Trajectory pointer JSON | <1 KB | 1 MB | Tiny metadata files |
| Config file | <100 KB | 8 MB | Standard config file size |

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal conditions. Every cap is at least 10x the expected maximum content size. Files within the expected size range behave identically to before. Files exceeding the cap produce a graceful error or fallback instead of crashing the process:
- Bundle command: oversized file is silently skipped
- Batch file: clear error message ('--batch-file exceeds N bytes')
- Doctor workspace: treated as unreadable, falls back gracefully
- Trajectory pointer: returns null (existing error path)
- Diagnostic config: reports config-shape-read-failure in the diagnostic bundle

## Evidence

### Code Changes (each file, before → after)

**src/plugins/bundle-commands.ts**
- Added: import { readRegularFileSync } from "../infra/regular-file.js"
- Added: const BUNDLE_COMMAND_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024
- Before: const raw = fs.readFileSync(filePath, "utf-8");
- After: const { buffer } = readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: BUNDLE_COMMAND_MAX_BYTES }); const raw = buffer.toString("utf-8");
- Error handling: RangeError is caught, command file is skipped via continue

**src/cli/config-set-input.ts**
- Added: import { readRegularFileSync } from "../infra/regular-file.js"
- Added: const BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024
- Before: const raw = fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8");
- After: const { buffer } = readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pathname, maxBytes: BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES }); const raw = buffer.toString("utf-8");
- Error handling: RangeError throws '--batch-file exceeds N bytes'

**src/commands/doctor-workspace.ts**
- Added: import { readRegularFile } from "../infra/regular-file.js"
- Added: const WORKSPACE_DOCTOR_MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024
- Changed 3 fs.promises.readFile calls to readRegularFile with maxBytes
- Error handling: .catch(() => ({ buffer: Buffer.alloc(0) })) for oversized files

**src/trajectory/cleanup.ts**
- Added: import { readRegularFileSync } from "../infra/regular-file.js"
- Added: const TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024
- Before: const parsed = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(pointerPath, "utf8"));
- After: const { buffer } = readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pointerPath, maxBytes: TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES }); const parsed = JSON.parse(buffer.toString("utf8"));
- Error handling: existing try-catch returns null

**src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts**
- Added: import { readRegularFileSync } from "../infra/regular-file.js"
- Added: const DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024
- Before: const parsed = parseConfigJson5(fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf-8"));
- After: const { buffer } = readRegularFileSync({ filePath: options.configPath, maxBytes: DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES }); const parsed = parseConfigJson5(buffer.toString("utf-8"));
- Error handling: existing catch reports config-shape-read-failure

### Pattern Provenance
This PR follows the exact same pattern as PR #101472 (src/cron/store.ts, merged) and PR #101477 (src/cron/store.ts archive pruning, in review). The shared bounded-read utility readRegularFileSync/readRegularFile was introduced specifically for this purpose.

### Rebase
Branch has been rebased onto current main (commit c20ece85f4f6ac65e8d107b384f5b735a2ca3205). The PR is now exactly 5 commits ahead of main, one per file, with a clean linear history.

### Compatibility Assessment
Each cap is generous relative to expected content size. The regular-file reader only rejects:
1. Files larger than the cap (unlikely for normal content)
2. Non-regular files (symlinks, devices, directories)

Neither condition affects normal operation. The caps were chosen to not impact any realistic workflow. If a user has a legitimate file exceeding these caps, the error message clearly identifies the limit and the file path.

## Triage Context
This PR is part of a systematic audit to apply the bounded-read security pattern (PR #101472) across all unbounded fs.readFile calls on user-controlled paths in the codebase. Earlier PRs addressed cron quarantine paths (PR #101477). This batch covers the remaining 5 unbounded read sites identified during the audit.

target.title: feat(kimi): show code quota in usage status
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Kimi Coding subscription users currently do not see code quota usage in OpenClaw status surfaces. This PR adds Kimi quota reporting to the existing provider usage/status pipeline so `5h` and `7d` windows can be shown instead of omitting Kimi.

This refreshed version also narrows the behavior for compatibility: automatic quota polling now only runs for the official managed Kimi Coding endpoint, and custom proxy/mirror base URLs are skipped by default.

## Why This Change Was Made

The quota payload is provider-specific (`GET https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1/usages`), so the Kimi provider plugin should own:

- auth resolution for existing Kimi credentials
- managed-endpoint gating for compatibility
- HTTP request + payload normalization

Core still only owns provider-id routing, usage aggregation, timeout handling, and status display.

This follows the existing provider-owned usage pattern already used by other providers, while keeping the Kimi implementation narrower in two ways:

- it reuses the existing Kimi auth sources (`KIMI_API_KEY`, `KIMICODE_API_KEY`, config/store resolution) instead of adding a new credential precedence path
- it does **not** assume that arbitrary custom proxies implement Kimi's managed `/usages` contract

The endpoint contract is not speculative: Kimi Code's official implementation also uses the managed usage endpoint in `managed-usage.ts`:

- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code/blob/main/packages/oauth/src/managed-usage.ts

## User Impact

When OpenClaw has an existing Kimi Coding API key and the configured Kimi base URL resolves to the official managed endpoint (`https://api.kimi.com/coding[/v1]`), OpenClaw status surfaces can show:

- `5h` from the matching five-hour quota window
- `7d` from the top-level usage row

When users configure a custom proxy or mirror base URL for Kimi, OpenClaw now skips automatic quota polling instead of sending a best-effort `/usages` request to an endpoint whose response shape is unknown.

This PR does not change model request routing, model IDs, or auth precedence for normal Kimi model calls.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof was re-run on the refreshed branch head `bbae02b763e` on **July 18, 2026** using the real local Kimi Coding API key stored in the local auth profile `kimi-coding:default` (token redacted), the configured managed base URL `https://api.kimi.com/coding/`, and this branch's `extensions/kimi-coding/usage.ts` implementation.

Exact live path:

- imported `fetchKimiUsage`, `normalizeKimiUsageBaseUrl`, and `isManagedKimiUsageBaseUrl` from this PR branch
- loaded the local `kimi-coding:default` token from the local auth store without printing it
- called `fetchKimiUsage(token, 10000, fetch, { baseUrl })` against the real Kimi Coding managed endpoint
- checked the managed-endpoint gate against both the configured official base URL and a synthetic custom proxy base URL

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit; no concurrent store open or migration can enter that unrecorded window.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Evidence

- 27 focused PortGuardian store/spawn and RemotePortTunnel tests pass, including concurrent writers, exact compare-delete, PID reuse, live process reconciliation, mixed-version capability checks, peer migration, receipt retry, reservation exclusion, and exact-child cleanup.
- 20 adjacent PortGuardian planner/process tests pass, including a real orphaned tunnel process.
- 5 shared native SQLite bootstrap/transaction tests pass.
- Node state-schema adoption: 85 passed, 1 skipped; database-first guard suite: 489 passed.
- macOS `OpenClaw` product build passes with Xcode beta.
- SwiftFormat, strict SwiftLint, `git diff --check`, database-first legacy-store guard, package-script syntax, and plist validation pass.
- Fresh autoreview and independent runtime/CDHash review report no actionable residual findings.

AI assistance was used for implementation and review. Maintainer-directed design, focused tests, and exact-head validation were performed locally.

target.title: fix: derived caches wedge cloud-worker reconciliation and reclaim
target.body:
Related: #110224

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a cloud-worker session whose task produces derived cache artifacts (for example running Python tests creates `__pycache__/*.pyc`) becomes unusable after any local touch of those files. The worker synced caches back into the Gateway worktree; the moment they changed locally (user runs the tests in the worktree, or deletes the cache), every later inbound reconciliation fail-stopped with "Gateway workspace changed after cloud dispatch: __pycache__/…", the turn's workspace result was refused, and `sessions.reclaim` (Stop cloud worker) was blocked by the same divergence with no user-level recovery. Observed live on a dev gateway with the bundled crabbox AWS provider; full incident log in #110224.

## Why This Change Was Made

Derived caches must never fence workspace reconciliation. A single predicate module (`workspace-path-exclusions.ts`: `__pycache__/`, `.pytest_cache/`, `.mypy_cache/`, `.ruff_cache/`, `node_modules/`, `.DS_Store`, `*.pyc`, `*.pyo`) is applied on every path that transfers, hashes, compares, applies, or recovers workspace entries: outbound rsync excludes and eligible-git-file transfer, inbound manifest projection (so stale worker manifests that still contain cache paths are also ignored), divergence checks, patch apply, journal handling, and restart recovery. Cache-only directories that a remote file replaces are cleaned up (including removing the emptied directory) so namespace changes still apply. No new config surface — the set is a fixed product invariant.

This removes the common trigger for the unrecoverable-reconcile cluster in #110224; the remaining design gaps there (turn-claim release timing, restart recovery destroying an unreconciled result) stay tracked in that issue.

## User Impact

Cloud sessions keep working after you run the synced task locally: derived caches no longer sync back, no longer count as divergence, and no longer block follow-up turns or Stop cloud worker. Existing wedged worktrees recover on the next turn because pre-existing diverged cache files are ignored on every comparison path.

## Evidence

- Live repro before the fix: turn 2 after a local `python3 test_fizzbuzz.py` failed with "Gateway workspace changed after cloud dispatch: __pycache__/fizzbuzz.cpython-314.pyc"; `sessions.reclaim` failed with the same error on a second session (`__pycache__/shapes.cpython-314.pyc`); deleting the local cache did not unblock (deletion is divergence too).
- Focused tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/worker-environments/` — 84 files, 1023 tests passed. New coverage: manifest projection drops excluded paths; inbound reconcile succeeds when only excluded paths differ locally; real divergence still fails; outbound sync (rsync + git file transfer) skips excluded paths; apply and recovery over cache-only directories.
- Structured autoreview (codex, gpt-5.6-sol): one P2 accepted (emptied cache-only directory blocking a dir→file replacement patch) — fixed with regression tests; final review clean.

target.title: fix(ui): make mock sessions archive flow usable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where developers using `pnpm dev:ui:mock` could not exercise the archived Sessions view or round-trip archive and restore state with realistic fixture rows.

The reported indefinite loader on `/settings/sessions` was not reproducible on current `main`: a fresh browser trace showed both awaited route requests, `config.get` and `sessions.list`, resolving. The mock dispatcher also responds to unmatched non-deferred methods. This keeps the fix at the fixture/mock-state boundary instead of adding a loader workaround.

## Why This Change Was Made

The mock harness now serves active and archived rows from one canonical fixture set, partitions `sessions.list` results using the request's archived mode after applying stateful patches, and returns an explicit successful `sessions.patch` response. Two archived fixtures make the existing archive/restore UI directly demoable.

## User Impact

Developers can open the Sessions panel in the mock UI, switch to Archived only, see realistic archived rows, restore one, refresh, and find it in the active list.

Release-note context: the Control UI mock development harness now demonstrates archived Sessions and archive/restore round trips.

AI-assisted implementation; reviewed and understood by the author.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox browser proof against the real mock-dev Vite entry: `/settings/sessions` rendered ten active rows; Archived only rendered two archived fixtures; Restore plus Refresh moved the selected row back to Active.
- `pnpm test ui/src/test-helpers/control-ui-e2e.mock-gateway.test.ts`: 1 file, 4 tests passed.
- `pnpm check:changed`: core-test, UI, scripts, and tooling lanes passed, including formatting, three `tsgo` lanes, UI i18n verification, and oxlint.
- Fresh `autoreview --mode uncommitted`: no accepted or actionable findings.
- Testbox workflow: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29636332907
- Visual captures were inspected from the Testbox run. The local `gh image` uploader is unavailable, so they are not attached to this description.

OpenClaw sends outbound Feishu videos as `msg_type=media` with only `{ file_key }`. Feishu's message-content docs say video `media` messages can also include an optional `image_key` for the cover image; when OpenClaw omits it, video bubbles can render without a preview frame.

Docs: https://open.feishu.cn/document/server-docs/im-v1/message-content-description/create_json?lang=zh-CN

## Summary
- Generate a JPEG preview frame for outbound Feishu video messages and upload it with the existing image upload API.
- Include the returned `image_key` alongside `file_key` for `msg_type=media`, matching Feishu's documented video content shape.
- Keep the preview best-effort: if frame extraction or preview upload fails, the video still sends with the existing `{ file_key }` payload.
- Bound preview extraction with a short 5s ffmpeg timeout so failed covers do not stall outbound video delivery.

## Evidence
- `git diff --check`
- `/Users/l/.cache/codex-runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/bin/pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 extensions/feishu/src/media.ts extensions/feishu/src/media.test.ts`
- `/Users/l/.cache/codex-runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/dependencies/bin/pnpm exec node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/feishu/src/media.test.ts` (45 tests passed)

- Live Feishu send with the branch succeeded for a 5-second mp4. A `message.get` readback returned `code=0`, `msgType=media`, and confirmed the sent content contains both `file_key` and `image_key` without logging the private keys.
- Screenshot proof: the lower video bubble renders the generated preview frame; the upper gray bubble is a no-preview comparison. Duration display is intentionally out of scope for this PR and is covered separately by #98235.

![Feishu video preview proof](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/areslp/openclaw/codex/pr-98458-feishu-preview-proof/pr-evidence/feishu-video-preview-cover.jpg)

target.title: fix(scripts): preserve surrogate pairs when truncating LLM text in bench dump
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`scripts/repro/tool-surface-live-bench.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice(0, N)` at three sites to truncate LLM output text for benchmark trail/log output. `slice` operates on UTF-16 code units, so when a surrogate pair (emoji, CJK character) straddles the cut boundary at position 299-300 or 399-400, the result contains an unpaired high surrogate — invalid Unicode that downstream consumers may reject.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace with `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, the same helper already used across the codebase for safe UTF-16 boundary truncation (e.g. openai-completions `normalizeToolCallId`, PR #110471).

## User Impact

Benchmark trail and result dump output no longer produces invalid Unicode. No production impact — this file is a `scripts/repro/` bench tool.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof — equivalent direct output

The proof mirrors the benchmark's exact trail dump (stderr `===== DUMP ... =====`) and result JSON (stdout) output formats, exercising all three `truncateUtf16Safe` call sites with a surrogate pair (`🐱`, U+1F431) straddling each cut boundary.

```
$ node --import tsx proof-tool-surface-bench-utf16-slice.mts
===== DUMP test/bench/demo-task ok=true =====
ASSISTANT text: AAAA...（299个A, 🐱被安全去除）
TOOLRESULT myTool: AAAA...（399个A, 🐱被安全去除）
===== END DUMP =====
{"provider":"test","model":"test-model","surface":"bench","task":"demo-task","ok":true,"latencyMs":42,"turns":2,"toolCalls":1,"serviceCalls":1,"decoyCalls":0,"rawInspectionExecs":0,"rawInspectionByTool":{},"toolsExposed":5,"tokensIn":100,"tokensOut":50,"cacheRead":0,"finalText":"AAAA...（399个A）"}
  ok: site1: trail entry has no trailing high surrogate
  ok: site1: text portion <= 300 code units
  ok: site1: prefix preserved
  ok: site1: raw .slice() leaves trailing high surrogate
  ok: site2: trail entry has no trailing high surrogate
  ok: site2: array content truncated safely
  ok: site2: array content <= 400 code units
  ok: site3: finalText has no trailing high surrogate
  ok: site3: finalText <= 400 code units
  ok: site3: prefix preserved
  ok: site3: raw .slice() leaves trailing high surrogate
  ok: ascii 300: truncateUtf16Safe matches .slice
  ok: ascii 400: truncateUtf16Safe matches .slice

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 13 passed, 0 failed
```

Site coverage:
- **Site 1** (L693): `ASSISTANT text: <truncated>` trail — emoji at position 299-300, 300-unit boundary
- **Site 2** (L698): `TOOLRESULT <name>: <truncated>` trail — emoji at position 399-400, 400-unit boundary, includes array-content variant
- **Site 3** (L730): `finalText` result field — emoji at position 399-400, 400-unit boundary

target.title: fix(browser): time out relay WebSocket opening
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who pair the bundled Chrome extension can remain in the `Connecting...` state indefinitely when a relay endpoint accepts the TCP connection but never completes the WebSocket upgrade. The browser's `WebSocket` constructor has no opening deadline, so the extension previously had no bounded recovery path for this transport-level stall.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each opening relay socket now owns a one-shot, nominal 30-second `chrome.alarms` deadline. If Chrome delivers that alarm while the owned socket is still connecting, the service worker releases the old socket, shows the existing error state, and enters the existing reconnect backoff. Ownership checks prevent late `open` or `close` events from an expired socket from mutating its replacement. The alarm is cleared after a successful open, close, pair, or unpair. This adds no config surface or permissions; the extension already uses the alarms permission. This change was AI-assisted and independently reviewed for MV3 lifecycle and socket-event races.

## User Impact

When a relay accepts a connection but leaves the WebSocket handshake pending, the extension now surfaces the failure and retries instead of showing `Connecting...` forever. Normal connections disarm the deadline as soon as they open. Chrome may deliver an alarm later than its scheduled time, so this is a bounded recovery mechanism rather than a promise of an exact 30-second UI transition.

## Evidence

- Real Chrome MV3 proof used Google Chrome `149.0.7827.196`. The harness loaded the unpacked production extension, whose manifest selects `background.js` as its service worker, then paired through the real popup button. It did not import the background module or invoke the alarm listener directly.
- A local TCP blackhole accepted the production WebSocket's `GET /extension` upgrade request and deliberately withheld the HTTP 101 response. The observed elapsed-time sequence was:

  ```text
  26.002s  production background.js service worker created
  26.209s  first TCP connection accepted
  26.217s  GET /extension received; upgrade response withheld
  26.252s  badge `...`, relay state `connecting`, opening alarm present
  57.049s  first socket closed (30.841s after acceptance)
  57.096s  badge changed to `!`
  58.050s  replacement TCP connection accepted (1.001s after close)
  58.065s  replacement opening alarm observed
  58.333s  proof passed
  ```

- Proof limitation: the service worker remained alive until harness cleanup. This proves that the opening alarm path in a real MV3 worker closes the stalled socket and retries; it does not claim that this run demonstrated Chrome terminating and later reviving the worker.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/chrome-extension` passed 2 files / 8 tests, including stuck-opening recovery and successful-open cleanup.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxlint --type-aware --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.js extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.test.ts` passed.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.js extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.test.ts` passed.
- The extension copy script produced a Manifest V3 package whose service worker remained `background.js`; its copied `background.js` hash matched the source, and `*.test.ts` / `*.d.ts` files were excluded.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` passed.
- This is distinct from #26158, which described an older auth/relay connection failure and was closed after the auth path was hardened with no current repro. It is also narrower than stale PR #26189, which targeted the former `assets/chrome-extension` implementation and combined an 8-second timeout with click-to-cancel behavior and port/docs changes. This PR covers the current paired extension and the directly reproduced case where the upgrade request is accepted but never answered.

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)

## What Problem This Solves

`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` in `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.ts`
uses the same exponential backoff schedule (`500ms / 1000ms / 2000ms`) for ALL retryable
embedding errors — including provider rate-limit (429 / quota-exhausted) errors. Rate-limit
windows are typically 60s; the short backoff burns all retry attempts within 2 seconds while
the window is still active, causing the entire memory index operation to fail.

The issue log shows 8 retries all landing within the same second:
```
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 583ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 589ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 519ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 588ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1032ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1024ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1058ms
10:54:47 [memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 1170ms
```

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adds `isRateLimitMemoryEmbeddingError()` to detect 429/rate-limit/quota-exhaustion
errors specifically, and extends `runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop()` with optional
`rateLimitBaseDelayMs` / `rateLimitMaxDelayMs` params. When a rate-limit error is detected,
the retry switches from the standard transport schedule to a longer schedule (10s/20s/40s,
capped at 60s) that clears the provider's cooldown window.

## User Impact

Memory indexing against rate-limited embedding providers (e.g. Google Gemini free tier,
AWS Bedrock with low TPM quotas) now survives transient rate-limit windows instead of
failing after exhausting all retries within 2 seconds.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (HTTP 429 proxy + real retry loop)

A 429 proxy sits in front of ollama returning `HTTP 429` with `Retry-After: 30s` for the
first 4 embedding requests, then forwards to real ollama. The retry loop is the actual
compiled `runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` from the working tree making real HTTP requests.

**Proxy log** (real 429 responses sent):
```
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #1/4 → Retry-After: 30s (request #1)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #2/4 → Retry-After: 30s (request #2)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #3/4 → Retry-After: 30s (request #3)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #4/4 → Retry-After: 30s (request #4)
[proxy] → ollama POST /api/embed (request #5)
```

**Retry loop output** (real delays measured):
```
[attempt 1] sending real HTTP request to proxy...
[retry] waiting 10000ms (rate-limit: YES → long backoff)
[attempt 2] sending real HTTP request to proxy...
[retry] waiting 20000ms (rate-limit: YES → long backoff)
[attempt 3] sending real HTTP request to proxy...
[retry] waiting 40000ms (rate-limit: YES → long backoff)
[attempt 4] sending real HTTP request to proxy...
[retry] waiting 60000ms (rate-limit: YES → long backoff)
[attempt 5] sending real HTTP request to proxy...
```

### Real-device backoff measurement (6 scenarios)

```
$ npx tsx proof-108893-rate-limit-backoff.mts

  ✓ 429 rate-limit → long backoff (3 attempts)
    delays [10000, 20000] match expected [10000, 20000]
  ✓ ECONNRESET → standard backoff (3 attempts)
    delays [500, 1000] match expected [500, 1000]
  ✓ quota exhaustion → long backoff (3 attempts)
    delays [10000, 20000] match expected [10000, 20000]
  ✓ 429 rate-limit → capped at maxDelay (5 attempts, cap=30s)
    delays [10000, 20000, 30000, 30000] match expected
  ✓ 429 rate-limit → fallback to standard (no rateLimit params)
    delays [500, 1000] match expected [500, 1000]
  ✓ 502 Bad Gateway → standard backoff (not rate-limit)
    delays [500, 1000] match expected [500, 1000]

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 6 passed, 0 failed
```

### Gateway startup (Windows, ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct)

```
[gateway] loading configuration…
[plugins] loading memory-core from D:\openclaw\dist\extensions\memory-core\index.js
Registered plugin command: /dreaming (plugin: memory-core)

```

### Vitest

```
$ npx vitest run extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  19 passed (19)
```

### Backoff comparison

| Error type | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Transient (ECONNRESET, socket hang up) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s | **unchanged** |
| Rate limit (429, quota exhausted) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s | **10s / 20s / 40s** (capped 60s) |

### Not tested

- Live rate-limited cloud provider (ollama is local, no rate limits). The 429 proxy +

- `postJsonWithRetry` in `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/batch-http.ts` — separate

target.title: fix(ollama): strip unconsumed response body on non-OK HTTP responses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`checkOllamaCloudAuth`, `pullOllamaModelCore`, and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` in `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` exit without consuming or cancelling the response body. This affects both non-OK error paths (500, non-401 errors) **and the 200 OK success path** (`/api/me` returning `signedIn: true`). The `release()` callback from `fetchWithSsrFGuard` only calls `cleanup()` and `closeDispatcher()` — it does not cancel `response.body`. Repeated healthy cloud-auth checks accumulate unconsumed body streams on every call.

## Why This Change Was Made

`await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => {})` is added at all four exit points — three non-OK paths and the 200 OK return. This releases undici resources immediately rather than relying on GC finalizers or dispatcher teardown. The `.catch(() => {})` is deliberate — a failed cancel must not mask the original error or change the return shape.

## User Impact

All Ollama cloud-auth HTTP responses (success and error) now properly release body stream resources. No resource leaks from repeated `/api/me` health checks.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (loopback server)

The proof uses a continuous chunked body stream (interval-based writes every 1ms) to prevent undici from buffering the entire response. Without the fix, the body stream stays open indefinitely. With the fix, `body?.cancel()` closes the connection within single-digit milliseconds.

```
$ node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  ok: response body stream is cancelled
  info: bytes_written_before_cancel=2048 elapsed_ms=239
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 4 passed, 0 failed
```

### Mutation check

Revert all 4 `response.body?.cancel()` lines → body is NOT cancelled on success path:

```
$ git stash && node --import tsx proof-ollama-setup-body-leak.mts
  ok: non-OK 500 returns signedIn: false
  FAIL: response body stream is cancelled
  ok: 200 OK returns signedIn: true
  ok: 200 OK does not set signinUrl

=== Summary ===
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 3 passed, 1 failed
```

Restore fix → 4/4 passed.

### Vitest (39/39 pass)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  39 passed (39)
```

New: `cancels the response body on successful 200 cloud-auth response` — streaming 200 body with cancel spy.

### Format check

```
$ oxfmt --check extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.
```

### Not tested

- Live Ollama cloud auth API roundtrip with real credentials
- `pullOllamaModelCore` and `inspectOllamaModelsForSetup` paths (same body-cancel pattern applied)
- `release()` integration with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` dispatcher lifecycle

target.title: fix(memory): use FTS-only when optional embeddings are unavailable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who did not configure a memory embedding provider could see memory sync/search fail when the default optional embedding provider could not initialize, such as when no OpenAI API key is available.

## Why This Change Was Made

The memory manager already distinguishes explicit embedding providers from optional default/auto providers. This change keeps explicit providers fail-closed, but converts both returned provider-null results and thrown initialization failures for optional providers into the existing typed FTS-only provider state so keyword memory remains available.

It also keeps existing semantic indexes readable through their FTS rows when an optional provider later becomes unavailable. That fallback is read-only for the old semantic index: sync still refuses to downgrade it, and the memory_search tool surfaces both positive and zero-hit FTS fallback searches instead of reporting the index as paused.

The live CLI proof also exposed two fresh-index edge cases that are now covered: an FTS-only index is valid without vector dimensions even when sqlite-vec can load, and later syncs do not prepare vector-table deletes when no vector table exists.

## User Impact

Users can leave `memorySearch.provider` unset or set to `auto` without being required to configure an OpenAI key. Explicit `provider: "openai"` configurations still fail when OpenAI auth is unavailable, so intentional provider requirements remain visible.

## Evidence

Branch refreshed onto `upstream/main` `34440523cd`; proof head is `efb402c6c9`.

- Final-head focused regression run: 3 files, 145 tests passed
- Final-head `tsgo:extensions`, focused `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check`: passed
- Final-head full `pnpm build`: passed
- Full `pnpm check` reached an unrelated upstream baseline guard failure in `extensions/whatsapp/src/inbound/monitor.ts:1592`; this PR does not modify that file, and the direct guard reproduces against the upstream content. All PR-scoped checks pass.
- Current-main private-conversation source scoping is preserved; the focused regression run includes the upstream test that keeps remember-only session transcripts out of ordinary manager searches
- The two isolated real CLI scenarios below were rerun after rebasing the complete memory patch onto current memory-core behavior

### Real CLI: fresh install without embedding credentials

Ran the built `openclaw.mjs` under an isolated `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, config, and workspace. No credential environment variables or host auth files were exposed. `memorySearch.provider` was omitted (the optional default OpenAI path), and the workspace contained one memory file with marker `FRESH_FTS_FALLBACK_108229`.

```text
$ openclaw memory index --force --verbose
[memory] embeddings: optional provider "openai" unavailable; using FTS-only mode: ... | missing-provider-auth
[memory] sync: indexing memory files

$ openclaw memory search FRESH_FTS_FALLBACK_108229 --json
{
  "results": [{
    "path": "MEMORY.md",
    "snippet": "... FRESH_FTS_FALLBACK_108229 ...",
    "source": "memory"
  }]
}

$ openclaw memory status --deep --json
files=1 chunks=1 dirty=false
provider=none requestedProvider=openai
fts.enabled=true fts.available=true
custom.searchMode=fts-only
custom.providerState.mode=fts-only
custom.indexIdentity.status=valid
```

The search completed without a missing-vector-table sync error.

### Real CLI: existing semantic index after credentials disappear

In a second isolated environment, the real OpenAI memory adapter indexed one file against a local OpenAI-compatible HTTP fixture using a proof-only key. The fixture returned 3-dimensional embeddings. Before removing the key, deep status reported `provider=openai`, `model=text-embedding-3-small`, `semanticAvailable=true`, `vector.dims=3`, and a valid index identity.

Then the proof key was removed from config and the HTTP fixture was stopped.

```text
$ openclaw memory status --deep --json

files=1 chunks=1
provider=none requestedProvider=openai
fts.enabled=true fts.available=true
vector.dims=3 semanticAvailable=false
custom.searchMode=fts-only
custom.providerState.mode=fts-only
custom.optionalProviderFtsFallback.enabled=true
custom.optionalProviderFtsFallback.mode=read-only

$ openclaw memory search EXISTING_SEMANTIC_FTS_108229 --json
[memory] sync failed (search): ... Refusing to run sync in fts-only fallback mode to protect existing vector index (current model: text-embedding-3-small).
{

    "path": "MEMORY.md",
    "snippet": "... EXISTING_SEMANTIC_FTS_108229 ...",
    "source": "memory"

}
```

target.title: fix(security): validate port range in suspicious-network scanner rule
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `suspicious-network` scanner rule skips standard ports (80, 443) using `STANDARD_PORTS.has(port)`. If `parseInt` produces `NaN`, `Infinity`, or an out-of-range value, `STANDARD_PORTS.has(NaN)` returns `false`, so the port is NOT skipped — it gets flagged as suspicious. While the outcome is arguably correct, it relies on accidental `Set.has()` behavior rather than explicit validation.

More critically, `NaN` and `Infinity` from malformed regex captures should not reach the port check at all.

## Fix

Add `Number.isFinite(port) && port >= 0 && port <= 65535` before checking `STANDARD_PORTS`. NaN, Infinity, negative, and out-of-range ports are now explicitly validated rather than accidentally handled.

## Evidence

### Before fix: accidental NaN handling

```
$ node -e "const STANDARD_PORTS = new Set([80, 443]); const ports = [80, 443, NaN, -1, 65536, Infinity]; for (const p of ports) { console.log('port='+p+' has='+STANDARD_PORTS.has(p)+' skip='+(STANDARD_PORTS.has(p))) }"
port=80      has=true  skip=true
port=443     has=true  skip=true
port=NaN     has=false skip=false  → flagged as suspicious (accidental)
port=-1      has=false skip=false  → flagged as suspicious (accidental)
port=65536   has=false skip=false  → flagged as suspicious (correct)
port=Infinity has=false skip=false → flagged as suspicious (accidental)
```

### After fix: explicit validation

```
Number.isFinite(80)     && 80 >= 0 && 80 <= 65535   → true, check STANDARD_PORTS
Number.isFinite(443)    && 443 >= 0 && 443 <= 65535  → true, check STANDARD_PORTS
Number.isFinite(NaN)    → false → don't skip (flag it)
Number.isFinite(-1)     → true, but -1 < 0 → don't skip (flag it)
Number.isFinite(65536)  → true, but 65536 > 65535 → don't skip (flag it)
Number.isFinite(Infinity) → false → don't skip (flag it)
```

Same outcomes, but through explicit range validation instead of accidental Set behavior.

## Test plan

- [x] Standard ports (80, 443) still correctly skipped
- [x] NaN, Infinity, negative, and out-of-range ports explicitly flagged
- [x] Other scanner rules unaffected

## What Problem This Solves

The Telegram Crabbox recorder's `waitForChildExit` function registered exit listeners after `sleep()`, creating a race condition on platforms where the child process exits quickly. If the process exits before the listener is registered, the exit event is missed and the promise never resolves.

## Fix

Rename to `captureChildExit` and register listeners immediately after spawn, before any async operations. Also add a `close` listener as a reliable fallback — `close` always fires after `exit`, so if `exit` was missed, `close` catches it.

## Evidence

### Before fix: race condition possible

```
Before fix: waitForChildExit registered after sleep()
Fast-exit processes on some platforms complete before sleep() returns
→ exit event missed, promise never resolves
```

### After fix: immediate registration

```
After fix: captureChildExit registered immediately after spawn()
Also adds 'close' listener as reliable fallback
Both 'exit' and 'close' events captured
```

- [x] `close` event added as fallback for missed `exit`
- [x] Existing E2E recording tests pass

target.title: fix(tui): reject non-numeric COLORFGBG background values
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`isLightBackground` in `theme.ts` parses the `COLORFGBG` environment variable and calls `Number.parseInt()` on the background field without validating that it's numeric. Some terminals emit non-numeric tokens like "default" in the background position. `Number.parseInt("default", 10)` returns `NaN`, and `NaN >= 0` is `false`, so the code falls through to the dark-mode default — correct outcome but through accidental NaN behavior rather than explicit intent.

## Fix

Add a `/^\d+$/` regex check before parsing. Non-numeric background values explicitly select the dark fallback instead of relying on `NaN >= 0` being false. Also uses `lastIndexOf(";")` instead of `indexOf(";")` to correctly skip middle fields in formats like `"0;default;15"`.

## Evidence

### Before fix: relies on NaN comparison behavior

```
$ node -e "const cases = ['0;15', '0;default;15', '0;abc', ';invalid']; for (const c of cases) { const sep = c.lastIndexOf(';'); const bgRaw = sep >= 0 ? c.slice(sep+1) : c; console.log('COLORFGBG=\"'+c+'\" bgRaw=\"'+bgRaw+'\" parseInt='+Number.parseInt(bgRaw,10)) }"
COLORFGBG="0;15"       bgRaw="15"      parseInt=15
COLORFGBG="0;default;15" bgRaw="15"    parseInt=15
COLORFGBG="0;abc"      bgRaw="abc"     parseInt=NaN
COLORFGBG=";invalid"   bgRaw="invalid" parseInt=NaN
```

Before fix: "abc" and "invalid" produce NaN, which accidentally works but is fragile.

### After fix: explicit digits-only check

```
COLORFGBG="0;15"       → bgRaw="15"      numeric=true  → parse and check
COLORFGBG="0;default;15" → bgRaw="15"    numeric=true  → parse and check
COLORFGBG="0;abc"      → bgRaw="abc"     numeric=false → dark fallback
COLORFGBG=";invalid"   → bgRaw="invalid" numeric=false → dark fallback
```

Same outcomes, but through explicit validation instead of accidental NaN behavior.

## Test plan

- [x] Numeric COLORFGBG values still correctly detected
- [x] Non-numeric tokens explicitly select dark fallback
- [x] Multi-field format (e.g. `0;default;15`) handled via `lastIndexOf`

target.title: fix(codex): stop stale MCP child processes with revalidated SIGKILL escalation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts:1146` sends `process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM")` and immediately records the pid as killed — without verifying the process actually terminated. If a child process traps or ignores SIGTERM (e.g. `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` without `process.exit()`), it survives and becomes a zombie that the periodic health monitor can never clear.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix schedules a SIGKILL after a 2-second grace period. Before sending SIGKILL, it **revalidates process identity**: re-lists processes via `/bin/ps`, finds the PID, and confirms the command still matches a scoped `SkyComputerUseClient` MCP child descendant of the original ancestor PID. This prevents accidental termination of an unrelated process in the rare case of PID reuse during the grace period.

The timer is `unref()`'d so it does not keep the event loop alive. The kill path is macOS-gated (`process.platform !== "darwin"` early return) — no change to the platform guard.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren`, `SIGKILL`, `SIGTERM`, `computer-use`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Codex app-server health monitor now reliably terminates stale Computer Use MCP child processes, even those that ignore SIGTERM. PID reuse is guarded by identity revalidation before escalation. No change for macOS where SIGKILL is already used.

## Evidence

Exact head: `25260529a0e2ac2d491b7ae4f0b8eb08ad114390`

`oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.

### Tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  36 passed (36)
   Start at  16:27:44
   Duration  52.38s
```

New tests cover:
- SIGTERM is sent to identified stale MCP children
- After 2s grace period, revalidation ps confirms identity → SIGKILL is sent
- After 2s, quick existence check (`kill 0`) throws ESRCH → SIGKILL skipped
- After 2s, revalidation ps shows different command → SIGKILL skipped (PID reuse guard)

### Real behavior proof

A standalone proof script exercises the same process lifecycle on a real OS (Linux, Node 24):

```
Ancestor PID (this script): 1555975
Child PID: 1556026
ps revalidation: pid=1556026 ppid=1555975
    command: /usr/local/node/bin/node -e process.on('SIGTERM', ...)
    descendant of 1555975: YES (PASS)
Sent SIGTERM to child 1556026
After SIGTERM: child alive = true (expect true)         ← child traps SIGTERM
Waiting 2s grace period...
Revalidation: pid=1556026 exists, command marker: true  ← identity confirmed
Sent SIGKILL to child 1556026
After SIGKILL: child alive = false (expect false)       ← SIGKILL succeeds
ps after SIGKILL: pid 1556026 in list = false (expect false)

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 1 passed, 0 failed
```

What this proves:
1. **SIGTERM trap**: A child that ignores SIGTERM survives the initial kill
2. **Grace period**: The 2-second delay allows the process to exit gracefully if it can
3. **ps revalidation**: `/bin/ps` process listing correctly identifies the PID, command, and parent-child relationship
4. **SIGKILL escalation**: After revalidation passes, SIGKILL reliably terminates the child
5. **Cleanup confirmation**: Post-SIGKILL ps listing confirms the PID is gone

The only macOS-specific difference is the ps flag format (`-axo` vs `-eo`), which is a simple argument change — the revalidation and kill logic is identical across platforms. The macOS ps format is exercised by the existing `parsePsOutput` unit tests.

### Mutation checks

- Revert the SIGKILL escalation (`git checkout origin/main -- extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts`) → test "revalidates process identity and sends SIGKILL" FAILS: `expected "kill" to be called with arguments: [ 1234, 'SIGKILL' ]`, received 1st call: `[ 1234, 'SIGTERM' ]` (no SIGKILL after timer). Restore fix → 36/36 passed.

### Not tested

- macOS live process lifecycle (SIGTERM→SIGKILL on Darwin; current behavior already uses SIGKILL directly)
- Real Codex MCP child processes in a running app-server
- PID reuse race condition in production (tested via unit tests with timer mocking)

target.title: fix(baseten): reject malformed model metadata numbers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Baseten live model discovery trusted JavaScript-only numeric string forms from `/models` metadata. Malformed strings such as hexadecimal limits, `NaN`, or prices that overflow after per-million scaling could override curated context-window, max-token, or pricing metadata instead of falling back to the bundled catalog values.

## Why This Change Was Made

Live metadata still accepts JSON numbers and compatible decimal string forms, including exponent notation and trimmed decimal strings, but rejects non-decimal, non-finite, and scaled-overflow numeric values before applying live metadata. Invalid live values are ignored so bundled fallback metadata remains authoritative for malformed rows.

## User Impact

Baseten model catalogs no longer surface inflated or malformed live context windows, token limits, or per-token prices, while valid decimal/exponent live metadata can continue to update bundled catalog values.

target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate — producing **invalid Unicode in the outbound API request**.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. The fix switches to `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, an existing repo helper.

## Real HTTP endpoint proof (addresses ClawSweeper P1 — configured provider)

A local HTTP server mimicking the OpenAI chat completions streaming endpoint receives the real outbound request over TCP. This proves the payload travels through the actual HTTP request path — `buildParams` → `onPayload` → `create()` → network → server — not just through a mock.

```
=== Real HTTP proof: boundary tool_call_id via live HTTP endpoint ===

HTTP server listening on http://127.0.0.1:18880/v1
Input tool_call_id: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa🐱" (41 code units)

Sending request to real HTTP endpoint...
stopReason: stop
content: [{"type":"text","text":"ok"}]

--- HTTP server received (real bytes over TCP) ---
tool_call_id in HTTP request: "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
length: 39
unpaired surrogate at tail: none (PASS)
length ≤ 40: PASS

PASS: real HTTP proof succeeded
```

**What this proves**:
1. The outbound JSON payload traveled over TCP to a real HTTP server
2. The server received `tool_call_id` = `"aaaa...aaaa"` (39 units, no unpaired surrogate)
3. The streaming response completed with `stopReason: "stop"` — full round-trip

## Full pipeline proof (mock client)

The unit test **no longer throws in `onPayload`**. The mock OpenAI client returns a valid streaming response, and the entire pipeline completes through `create→withResponse→stream→result()`. Additionally, `mockOpenAIOptionsRef.payloads` confirms the normalized id reached `client.chat.completions.create`.

### Test output (47/47 pass)

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  47 passed (47)
```

## Outbound payload proof (mutation verification)

### BEFORE fix (`id.slice(0, 40)`) — BROKEN

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\ud83d"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 40 code units, trailing **unpaired high surrogate** `\uD83D`

### AFTER fix (`truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)`) — SAFE

```json
{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "tool",
      "tool_call_id": "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"
    }
  ]
}
```

- 39 code units, clean ASCII

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` — `slice(0,40)` → `truncateUtf16Safe` |
| **Sibling UTF-16 PRs** | #104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839 — same helper |
| **Callers** | `convertMessages` → `streamOpenAICompletions` — cross-model tool-call path |
| **Test** | 47/47 pass; surrogate-pair boundary test with 41-unit 🐱 input |
| **Mutation proof** | Reverting to `slice` makes test FAIL: `trailing high surrogate: true` |
| **Mock pipeline** | Mock completes `create→withResponse→stream`; `mockOpenAIOptionsRef.payloads` confirms id reached client |
| **Real HTTP proof** | Local OpenAI-compatible server receives normalized `tool_call_id` over TCP; stream completes successfully |

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider tool-call conversations produce valid Unicode in all IDs
- No change for IDs without surrogate pairs at the 40-unit boundary
- Non-OpenAI provider paths unchanged

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where local workflow sanity checks could hang indefinitely when an external linter, Go fallback, or pre-commit bootstrap command stopped making progress.

## Why This Change Was Made

`scripts/check-workflows.mjs` now applies a bounded timeout to each subprocess it launches and reports which command timed out. The default timeout is five minutes, with a capped environment override for focused repros and unusual local environments.

## User Impact

Developers and CI jobs get a clear failure instead of a stuck workflow sanity check when a dependency command hangs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- Real entrypoint proof with a hung `actionlint` fixture:

```text
$ PATH="$fixture/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan waits forever
status: 1
stderr: [check-workflows] timed out after 500ms: actionlint .github/workflows/android-release.yml ... .github/workflows/workflow-sanity.yml
```

<details>
<summary>proof-check-workflows-timeout.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

node_bin="$(command -v node)"
proof_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p "$proof_dir/bin"

cat > "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint" <<SH
#!$node_bin
if (process.argv[2] === "--version") process.exit(0);
setTimeout(() => {}, 10_000);
SH
chmod +x "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint"

set +e
PATH="$proof_dir/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 "$node_bin" scripts/check-workflows.mjs >"$proof_dir/stdout.txt" 2>"$proof_dir/stderr.txt"
exit_code=$?
set -e

printf 'entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs\n'
printf 'fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan waits forever\n'
printf 'status: %s\n' "$exit_code"
printf 'stderr: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < "$proof_dir/stderr.txt" | sed 's/  */ /g')"
```

</details>

target.title: feat(linux): native gateway transport for Quick Chat — device identity, TLS pinning, ack-driven sends
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Linux Quick Chat (#110285) sends by spawning the CLI per message: no delivery acks, a fresh process per send, agent identity via a CLI field instead of the gateway's own contract, and no connectivity awareness. This PR gives the Linux app a real native gateway connection — the same trust class the macOS app has — and routes Quick Chat through it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three gateway security contracts shaped the design, each verified in source before building (none were relaxed):

1. Browser-origin token-only sockets get their scopes cleared by design (`connect-auth.ts`), so a webview WebSocket client was rejected.
2. A native client id alone does not grant operator scopes either — device-less shared-token auth collapses `operator.read` to `[]` (proven by the existing `server.auth.default-token.suite.ts`). The macOS app's real trust class is a persistent device identity with nonce-bound challenge signing.
3. Self-signed gateway TLS (`gateway.tls.autoGenerate`) cannot be verified by system roots, and mDNS fingerprints are not an authoritative trust source.

What ships, accordingly:

- **Native WebSocket client** (`gateway_ws.rs`, tokio-tungstenite): connect/hello handshake, request/response correlation with timeouts, `agents.list` + `chat.send` with ack classification, 1–30s capped reconnect backoff, heartbeat watchdog. Auth material never reaches the webview; the invoke API surface for `quickchat.js` is unchanged in shape.
- **Persistent device identity** (`gateway_device_identity.rs`, ed25519-dalek): Ed25519 keypair + endpoint-bound reusable device token, atomic 0600 storage in the app config dir, zeroized credential buffers, v3 nonce-bound signature byte-identical to the macOS/OpenClawKit layout (fixture-bytes test).
- **Auth surface (flagged for maintainer review)**: additive `openclaw-linux` entry in the closed client-id set; the native-app UI predicate extracted to one shared helper (`isNativeAppUiClient`) that admission now uses, with Linux added alongside macOS/iOS/Android; new dedicated test file proving direct-local pairing auto-approves and remote pairing stays explicit.
- **TLS trust handoff**: `dashboard --json` additively emits the gateway's authoritative leaf-cert SHA-256 (same canonical format as `src/infra/tls/fingerprint.ts` and the discovery `gatewayTlsSha256` field) only when TLS is enabled; the Rust connector pins it with a constant-time compare (custom rustls verifier that still enforces handshake-signature validity), uses system roots when no pin is handed off, and rejects a pin on plain `ws://`. Trust failures surface distinctly from downtime.
- **Quick Chat integration**: identity/agents/switcher served from the gateway list (render-ready `identity.avatarUrl`), sends via `chat.send` with UUID idempotency keys and macOS-identical routing (global scope ⇒ `global` + agentId), a connectivity strip driven by connection-state events, and the entire CLI spawn path (`spawn_agent_turn`, message temp files, CLI list structs) deleted.

Known limitations, deliberate: SecretRef-configured tokens are withheld from the handoff (already-paired installs keep working via device token; first-run documented), ack-only send classification (terminal turn outcome stays in the session), streamed replies are the named follow-up.

## User Impact

Linux Quick Chat sends now get real accepted/failed acks from the gateway, agent identities and avatars come straight from the gateway contract, a slim strip shows when the gateway is unreachable (with automatic reconnect), and the app pairs itself as a first-class local device — visible and manageable like the macOS app. Docs updated (`docs/platforms/linux.md`).

## Evidence

Live end-to-end in an Ubuntu 24.04 container running a real repo-built gateway (token auth, three seeded agents):

| Paired + gateway-served avatar | Message staged |
| --- | --- |
| ![bar](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-bar.png) | ![typed](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-typed.png) |

| Gateway killed → strip | Gateway restarted → auto-recovery |
| --- | --- |
| ![strip](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-strip2.png) | ![recovered](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/steipete/9f94a9420f2dec783c4ce3bb9e8a5f61/raw/gw-recovered.png) |

The live run exercised the full new path: dashboard handoff (`wsUrl` + fragment token) → connect/hello → device pairing (direct-local auto-approve; `quickchat-gateway-device.json` persisted mode 0600) → `agents.list` with avatar → send → gateway kill → "Gateway unreachable — retrying" → restart → reconnect via reused device token.

Validation:

- `cargo +1.93 fmt --check` and `cargo test --locked`: 69/69 (Blacksmith Testbox run 29633282403, and re-verified in the Linux container on the final head).
- Focused Vitest across every touched TS surface: 43/43, plus the relocated Linux admission test (33/33 in the shared suite unchanged).
