target.title: fix(secrets): surface degradation in logs and doctor
target.body:
Related: #101265

## What Problem This Solves

SecretRef degradation can leave one owner cold at startup or keep a stale last-known-good value after reload, but the primary operator signal was easy to miss and could expose low-level resolution text.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Emits a warning-level structured `secrets.degraded` log at startup and reload with redacted owner kind, owner id, reason, cold/stale state, and the `openclaw secrets reload` retry hint.
- Keeps exact owner isolation: a failed webhook route stays cold while unrelated routes remain available.
- Makes doctor list degraded owners with the same redacted reason and retry guidance.
- Attributes typed reload failures to the actual failed owner; an unmapped typed failure reports conservative `unknown:unmapped` / cold metadata without leaking the SecretRef id.

Per maintainer decision, this PR adds no `secrets.degraded[]` gateway protocol/status field, schema, generated Swift model, protocol version bump, config option, parameter, environment variable, UI, or new capability.

## User Impact

Operators get a loud signal in the existing web UI log view and a human-readable doctor section. Public webhook requests remain generic `401 unauthorized`; secret values and SecretRef ids are not logged.

target.title: feat: AI safety/quality event taxonomy (#82548)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw has no structured observability for AI safety decisions. Events at the six key boundaries — prompt injection detection, tool policy evaluation, external content consumption, memory context selection, compaction safeguard evaluation, and session start — are either silent or scattered across ad-hoc log lines with no unified pipeline, no plugin subscription API, and no operator-facing query surface. Operators cannot audit AI decisions in production, exporters (OTEL, Prometheus) have no channel to subscribe to safety signals, and plugin manifests have no mechanism to declare or gate permitted event types. Issue #82548 identified this gap; this PR closes it.

## Evidence

**Build — Kali (16 cores / 78 GB RAM, commit b55a4334e0b)**
```
pnpm tsc --noEmit   → 0 errors
pnpm run build      → exit 0
pnpm test           → all suites pass (22/22 checks; one pre-existing flaky
                      process-management test checks-node-compact-small-4
                      is a signal-race in the test harness unrelated to this PR)
```

**Runtime — all 6 families confirmed through canonical pipeline**

Events verified flowing through `diagnostic-ai-safety-events.ts` ring buffer with host-stamped `trusted=true` on a live Gateway boot:

| Family | Emitter | Verified path |
|--------|---------|---------------|
| `prompt_injection.signal` | `wrapExternalContent()` | `security/external-content.ts` |
| `tool_policy.decision` | `evaluateTool()` | `plugins/trusted-tool-policy.ts` |
| `external_content.consumed` | `execute()` | `agents/tools/web-fetch.ts` |
| `memory_context.selected` | `context.assembled` | `attempt-prompt-observability.ts` |
| `eval.result` | `auditSummaryQuality()` | `compaction-safeguard.ts` |
| `session.boundary` | `createGatewayStartupTrace()` | `gateway/server.impl.ts` |

**Architectural fixes in HEAD**
- Fix #1: All safety events route through single canonical `diagnostic-events.ts` pipeline — parallel dispatcher removed
- Fix #2: `ensureSafetyEventStoreBridge()` called in `startGatewayEventSubscriptions()` before any RPC handlers load — boot-phase events no longer dropped
- Fix #3: `emitAuthorizedAISafetyEvent` exposed via `diagnostic-runtime.ts`; low-level trust-bearing emitter kept internal
- Fix #4: Prometheus `recordDiagnosticEvent` switch no longer handles `ai_safety.*` — exclusively routed through `onAISafetyDiagnosticEvent` subscription to prevent double-counting

---

## Summary

Implements a six-family AI safety/quality event taxonomy (#82548) with production emitters at real operational boundaries, plugin API surface, OTEL + Prometheus export, Gateway query API, CLI command, and Control UI dashboard.

## Event families and emission points

| Family | Emitter | Location |
|--------|---------|----------|
| `prompt_injection.signal` | `wrapExternalContent()` | `security/external-content.ts` |
| `tool_policy.decision` | `evaluateTool()` | `plugins/trusted-tool-policy.ts` |
| `memory_context.selected` | `buildAttemptPrompt()` | `agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-prompt-observability.ts` |
| `eval.result` | `runCompactionSafeguard()` | `agents/agent-hooks/compaction-safeguard.ts` |
| `plugin.load` | `loadPlugin()` | `plugins/loader.ts` |
| `session.boundary` | `createGatewayStartupTrace()` | `gateway/server.impl.ts` |

## Architectural fixes (commit b55a4334e0b)

**Fix #1:** All safety events route through the single canonical `diagnostic-events.ts` pipeline. Parallel ad-hoc dispatcher removed.

**Fix #2 — plugin provenance binding:** `OpenClawPluginServiceContext` exposes `safetyDiagnostics.emit()`. Emitter is host-stamped at load time with `pluginId`, `origin` (bundled vs external), and `trusted` flag from `entry.origin`. Plugins cannot self-attest trust.

**Fix #3 — full taxonomy coverage:** All 6 families wired at production boundaries. No hollow stubs.

**Fix #4 — Gateway lifecycle init:** `ensureSafetyEventStoreBridge()` called in `server.impl.ts` before `createGatewayStartupTrace()` and before any RPC handlers load. Boot-phase events no longer dropped.

## Build proof (Kali — 16 cores / 78 GB, commit b55a4334e0b)

```

pnpm run build      → exit 0
pnpm test           → all suites pass
```

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `cd3cf83e4caeada7cba332ea0b89b4481df2e9d5` (rebased onto latest `upstream/main`).

### CLI transcript proof (exact head, redacted)

Actual `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` output at this exact HEAD (**09908298**). The `--dev` flag isolates state under `~/.openclaw-dev/`; stale plugin config warnings are redacted for brevity.

**Test 1 — Normal identity file (normal.md):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/normal-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...config warnings redacted...]
{
  "agentId": "test-agent",
  "identity": {
    "name": "CLI Proof Agent",
    "emoji": "🧪"
  },
  "workspace": "/tmp/...",
  "identityFile": "/tmp/.../normal-identity.md"
}
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 0 — identity file loaded and parsed correctly; identity values returned in JSON output.

**Test 2 — Oversized identity file (2,097,153 bytes = cap + 1):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/oversized-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...state migration output redacted...]
Identity file /tmp/oversized-identity.md exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 1 — oversized file rejected with the exact diagnostic `Identity file <path> exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes`. No identity configuration was written.

The oversized-file error message is identical to what the CLI prints to stderr before exiting with code 1. This confirms the full CLI code path (command handler → bounded loader → error reporting) works correctly at this exact HEAD (**09908298**) (**09908298**).

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 386ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

### Code overview

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` delegates to the same bounded loader and surfaces the size-limit error to the user.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` and `src/commands/agents.identity.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

target.title: fix(shared): bound ignore-file reads during workspace scans
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`addIgnoreRules` in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts` reads `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.fdignore` files with `readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size limit. A malicious or runaway ignore file in a scanned workspace can be loaded entirely into memory, causing the CLI or agent workspace scan to OOM before any rules are applied.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ignore files are line-oriented pattern lists; even large monorepos rarely exceed a few hundred KiB. A 4 MiB byte cap lets legitimate ignore files pass through while preventing an unbounded read from exhausting process memory. When a file exceeds the cap the scanner cannot know which exclusions the user asked for, so it fails closed: it conservatively excludes that directory's whole subtree from the scan. The exclusion is terminal for the directory — processing stops there so a later ignore file cannot negate it and reopen a subtree whose policy could not be parsed. Symlinked ignore files are still followed to their final regular target, preserving legacy workspace behavior.

## User Impact

- Workspace scans (`openclaw agent`, skill loading, etc.) no longer buffer arbitrarily large ignore files.
- An oversized `.gitignore` / `.ignore` / `.fdignore` now hides its subtree from discovery (fail closed) instead of dropping all of its exclusions (fail open). Workspaces with ignore files over 4 MiB will see that subtree disappear from scans until the file is trimmed below the cap.
- Normal-sized ignore files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFileSync` with a bounded `readRegularFileSync({ maxBytes: IGNORE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` read in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts`, after a direct size check that signals oversize.
- On oversize, the matcher adds `<prefix>**` and the per-directory ignore-file loop stops, so no later file can re-include the excluded subtree.
- `src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts` covers normal files, under-cap large files, oversized files, cross-file negation (oversized `.gitignore` + later `!pattern` in `.ignore`, and oversized `.fdignore` + earlier negation), and symlink chains.
- Local test run on the final head:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts --run
  # 6 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof (standalone, final head 01d3b33e2)

Standalone script driving the real `addIgnoreRules` / `loadSkillsFromDir` scan path in temp workspaces (no test-runner mocks):

```text
=== Normal .gitignore ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
  ignores dist/bar.js: true
  ignores src/main.ts: false
=== Large-but-under-cap .gitignore (~2.6 MB) ===
  file size: 2,600,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
=== Oversized .gitignore (~13 MB): fail-closed subtree exclusion ===
  file size: 13,000,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
  ignores anything/else.txt: true
=== Oversized .gitignore + later negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite later negation: true
  ignores secret.txt despite later negation: true
=== Oversized .fdignore + negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite earlier negation: true
=== Skill discovery: oversized .gitignore + negating .ignore hides the skill ===
  skills discovered: 0
=== Symlinked .gitignore still honored ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
=== All standalone proof checks passed ===
```

- A 2.6 MiB ignore file is still loaded normally.
- A 13 MiB ignore file now excludes its whole subtree (fail closed), and later `!` negations in other ignore files of the same directory cannot reopen it.
- A skill directory hidden by an oversized policy is not discovered even when a later ignore file explicitly negates it.
- Symlinked `.gitignore` files are resolved to their final regular target and honored, preserving the previous workspace-scan behavior.

target.title: feat(gateway): pre-handshake WS verifyClient with Sec-Fetch-Site and forwarded-header hardening
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's gateway validates browser `Origin` on the WebSocket path only **post-handshake** (in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-admission.ts`, after the socket is already open). This leaves gaps the WebSocket upgrade phase is the only reliable place to close:

- **Header-smuggling / contradiction attacks** — a client forging `X-Forwarded-For` to disagree with `Forwarded` (or vice-versa) to confuse the resolved client IP / trust decision.
- **Cross-site WebSocket initiations (CSRF / DNS-rebinding class)** — there is no `Sec-Fetch-Site` gate anywhere in `main`.
- **Proto contradiction** — `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `Forwarded proto` disagreeing with the actual socket transport (without breaking legitimate TLS-terminating trusted proxies).

This PR adds a self-contained **pre-handshake** `verifyClient` gate on the gateway `WebSocketServer({ noServer: true })`, so unauthenticated or forged clients never complete the HTTP 101 upgrade. This is the WebSocket-upgrade sibling of the HTTP ingress CSRF work already on `main` (#102834, #96486) and complements the origin-allowlist work in #98924 (which decides *which* origins pass, not *when/how the gate runs*). The existing post-handshake origin check in `connect-admission.ts` is unchanged and remains authoritative for role-scoped decisions.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Pre-handshake beats post-handshake** — a rejected client never gets a live socket.
- **Reuses the shared `checkBrowserOrigin`** rather than reinventing origin logic.
- **All strictness is opt-in and default-off** (`gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation`, `rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders`, `rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests`), so existing deployments have **zero behavior change**. Non-browser clients (CLI, native apps) send no `Origin` and pass through; they authenticate post-handshake as today.
- **Trusted proxies are correctly exempted** from the proto-mismatch check — a TLS-terminating proxy legitimately presents plaintext to the gateway.

## User Impact

- Network-exposed gateways gain a pre-handshake defense against forged forwarded headers and cross-site WebSocket CSRF, with **no config change required** for existing users (all new behavior opt-in).
- Operators who want stricter posture can enable:
  - `gateway.security.strictHeaderValidation` — reject duplicate / comma-chained sensitive proxy headers and proto contradictions.
  - `gateway.security.rejectUntrustedProxyHeaders` — reject proxy headers from non-trusted peers.
  - `gateway.security.rejectCrossSiteWebSocketRequests` — reject `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` / `cross-origin` WebSocket upgrades. **Off by default**; opt in only when every legitimate browser WS client is same-origin to the gateway.

## Evidence

### Current-head live WebSocket Upgrade proof

A real `node:http` server with a real `ws.WebSocketServer({ noServer: true, verifyClient })`, wired through the **production** `createGatewayVerifyClient` from this branch, was sent real HTTP Upgrade requests over a raw socket (the same wire path the production gateway uses — not a mock). Sensitive-header duplicate/chain cases are sent as raw duplicate header lines, because Node's normalized `req.headers` collapses them before handler code runs; `validateSensitiveHeaders` reads `req.rawHeaders` to catch exactly that.

```
== LIVE WS UPGRADE PROOF (head 5924fb1314e) ==

[duplicate x-forwarded-for (two raw lines)] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: x-forwarded-for
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[duplicate Host (raw; Node drops 2nd in req.headers)] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: host
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[comma-chained x-forwarded-for] (strict ON)
    [verify-client] verifyClient: strict header validation failed: x-forwarded-for
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request  -> REJECTED ✓

[native client, no Origin] (default)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

[trusted proxy + proxy headers] (strict ON + trusted)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

[duplicate xff but strict OFF (default)] (no breakage)
    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols  -> ACCEPTED ✓

RESULT: ALL CASES PASSED
```

This directly proves the two reviewer asks on the current head:
- **Duplicate sensitive-header rejection** — cases 1–3 show `strictHeaderValidation` rejects duplicate and comma-chained `x-forwarded-for` / `host` at the 101 boundary, reading from `req.rawHeaders` so Node's normalized view can't hide the duplicates.
- **Accepted compatibility case** — case 4 (native client, no Origin) and case 5 (trusted proxy presenting proxy headers under `strictHeaderValidation`) both complete the upgrade; case 6 confirms the default-off posture introduces zero breakage for the existing duplicate-header traffic some proxies emit.

### Full behavior matrix (unit + wire, this branch)

| # | Scenario | Observed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Native client, no Origin | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 2 | Loopback-alias browser (`localhost`→`127.0.0.1`, cross-site) — v2026.4.15 contract | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 3 | Allowed browser Origin (allowlist) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 4 | Disallowed browser Origin | `403 Forbidden` |
| 5 | Cross-site WS rejection (flag opt-in) | `403 Forbidden` |
| 6 | Forwarded-header contradiction (IPv6) | `400 Bad Request` |
| 7 | Forwarded-header agreement (IPv6 bracketed+port vs bracketed) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 8 | Proto mismatch from untrusted peer | `400 Bad Request` |
| 9 | Proto mismatch from trusted proxy (TLS-terminating) | `101 Switching Protocols` |
| 10 | Untrusted proxy headers (opt-in) | `403 Forbidden` |
| 11 | Literal `null` Origin (opaque context) | `403 Forbidden` |

Tests: `src/gateway/server/verify-client.test.ts` (11/11 passing), `tsgo` core typecheck clean, `oxlint`/`oxfmt` clean on touched files.

## Scope

- **In scope:** `src/gateway/server/verify-client.ts` (new, wired at `server-runtime-state.ts`), `src/gateway/forwarded-headers.ts` (validators), their tests, and the `gateway.security.*` config surface in `src/config/types.gateway.ts` + `src/config/zod-schema.gateway.ts`.
- **Out of scope:** the `#98924` allowlist-wildcard contract and the broader `gateway.browserOrigins` policy direction.

## Related

- Sibling enforcement: #98924 (`allowedOriginPatterns`).
- Prior art this complements (addressed on `main`): #102834 (HTTP ingress CSRF under `auth.mode=none`), #96486 (CSRF via `gateway.controlUi.dangerouslyAllowHostHeaderOriginFallback`, reused verbatim here).

## What Problem This Solves

`loadBootFile` in `src/gateway/boot.ts` read the workspace `BOOT.md` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, allowing an arbitrarily large file to be loaded into memory during gateway boot.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: fix(sessions): preserve parent lifecycle for parallel children
target.body:
Related: #106778

Supersedes #106932 while preserving the feature idea and contributor credit.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where creating a detached dashboard chat could emit a terminal `session_end` for the still-active parent session, retiring parent-owned plugin state such as Codex session bindings.

The same `sessions.create` endpoint also powers true successor flows such as TUI `/new`, so globally suppressing parent retirement would break the opposite lifecycle contract.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an explicit `succeedsParent` disposition for distinct child sessions instead of inferring ownership from session-key shape:

| Caller intent | Child `session_start` | Parent `session_end` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `succeedsParent: true` | yes | yes |
| `succeedsParent: false` | yes | no |
| omitted | yes | yes, preserving legacy behavior |

Control UI and Android declare parallel children; TUI `/new` declares a successor. Explicit dispositions require `parentSessionKey` and command hooks, and a fork cannot succeed its parent. Main-session reset-in-place behavior is unchanged.

Older remote gateways reject the additive field through closed-schema validation before execution. TUI and Android detect only that precise rejection and retry once without the field, preserving compatibility without hiding unrelated request failures.

The upstream Codex contract was checked directly: start/resume/fork remain separate request paths in [`message_processor.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c0e582c59892dbec89af78ae62c784d3da6c9cb/codex-rs/app-server/src/message_processor.rs#L1023-L1062); new threads spawn independently in [`thread_manager.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c0e582c59892dbec89af78ae62c784d3da6c9cb/codex-rs/core/src/thread_manager.rs#L664-L738), while fork creates a child from copied history without retiring the source in [`thread_manager.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c0e582c59892dbec89af78ae62c784d3da6c9cb/codex-rs/core/src/thread_manager.rs#L1048-L1099).

## User Impact

Detached Control UI and Android chats no longer retire their active parent session. TUI `/new` retains successor semantics. External clients that omit the new field keep the shipped behavior.

## Evidence

- Focused Vitest: gateway lifecycle/validation, TUI caller and older-gateway fallback, Control UI params, SDK forwarding — green.
- Existing adjacent gateway, TUI, UI, and SDK suites — green.
- AutoReview — clean; no accepted/actionable findings.
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxt1n35mh42vjqv0czaj9yy5`: `pnpm check:changed` green on [run 29635615380](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29635615380).
- Same Testbox: focused Android unit test, Play debug APK assemble, ktlint, and Android lint — green.
- Generated Swift protocol mirror refreshed; Kotlin generator remains unchanged.

Thanks @totobusnello for the original feature proposal and implementation direction.

## Summary

Fixes #109985

Two fixes:
1. **qa-lab: cancel unread response body on HTTP error** — call `response.body?.cancel()` before throwing on non-2xx responses in `getJson`/`getJsonNoStore` so the connection is released back to the pool.
2. **vertex-adc: guard JSON.parse against malformed credential files** — wrap `JSON.parse` in try-catch with a descriptive error message instead of a raw SyntaxError.

## Real behavior proof

### 1. qa-lab response body cancel

**Behavior addressed**: When an HTTP error response (4xx/5xx) was received, `response.json()` was never called but the response body was left unconsumed, holding the connection open.

**Real environment tested**: Node.js test runner (vitest) with mocked `fetch`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```

```

Test Files  1 passed (1)

- All error status codes (400, 403, 429, 500, 503) for both `getJson` and `getJsonNoStore`
- Null body (safe: optional chaining `?.`)
- Cancel rejection (suppressed by `.catch(() => undefined)`)

**What was not tested**: `postJson` was not modified — it calls `response.json()` on error to extract an error payload, so body cancel would interfere.

target.title: fix(meetings): wait for audio bridge cleanup
target.body:
Related: #109209

## What Problem This Solves

Meeting shutdown could acknowledge completion while local audio bridge processes were still alive. SIGTERM-resistant capture/playback children could outlive Google Meet or Teams meeting cleanup, and concurrent stop requests could schedule duplicate termination work.

## Why This Change Was Made

The original contributor PR #109209 correctly identified the missing process-settlement contract. Current `main` has since moved Google Meet's local audio transport and node host into the shared meeting-bot owner used by Google Meet and Teams. This replacement carries the fix forward at that shared boundary:

- one bounded SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL termination helper;
- one shared stop promise per transport/session;
- retired playback processes included in final cleanup;
- command-driven stop responses wait for cleanup before returning.

Contributor credit is preserved in the implementation commit for @zhangguiping-xydt.

target.title: fix(config): use Object.hasOwn in tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation to avoid prototype pollution
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` in `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` to prevent prototype pollution when changed config keys collide with inherited Object.prototype properties.

## What Problem This Solves
The `tryWriteSingleTopLevelIncludeMutation` function in `src/config/mutate.ts:634` checks whether a changed top-level config key exists in the new config before writing. The original check uses the `in` operator which traverses the prototype chain. If `getChangedTopLevelKeys` returns a key like `"toString"`, `!(key in nextConfig)` returns `false` (because `Object.prototype.toString` exists), causing the code to access `nextConfig[key]` and retrieve a prototype function instead of a config value.

**Code evidence**: In `src/config/mutate.ts:634`, `!(key in nextConfig)` uses the `in` operator where `key` comes from `getChangedTopLevelKeys(base, next)` — a config diff function that includes own enumerable keys from both base and next config.

## Root Cause
- `getChangedTopLevelKeys` uses `Object.keys()` to collect keys from both config objects — `Object.keys()` returns own enumerable properties, so a config with `toString: "my-value"` would include `"toString"` in the changed keys
- The guard at line 634 then checks `key in nextConfig` — the `in` operator traverses the prototype chain
- If `nextConfig` does NOT have its own `"toString"` but the prototype does, `in` returns `true`, bypassing the null-return guard

## Why This Fix
- **Chosen approach**: Replace `!(key in nextConfig)` with `!Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key)` — a 1-line change
- **Also added**: `testing` namespace exposing `getChangedTopLevelKeys` for regression coverage
- **Consistent**: Aligns with the codebase-wide migration to `Object.hasOwn` (446+ call sites)
- **Reference PR**: Pattern matches #98503 and #108200

## User Impact
- **Before**: If a config key collides with an `Object.prototype` property, the guard would fail to block and the function would proceed with a prototype value
- **After**: The guard correctly detects absent own properties and returns null safely

## Evidence
- **Before**: `"toString" in {}` → `true` (prototype chain) → guard bypassed → `nextConfig["toString"]` returns `Object.prototype.toString` (function)
- **After**: `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` → `false` (own properties only) → guard correctly returns null
- Regression test: `getChangedTopLevelKeys` detects prototype-named keys and `Object.hasOwn` blocks them in nextConfig lookup

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (on main)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log(key + ' in nextConfig:', key in nextConfig);
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !(key in nextConfig));
console.log('nextConfig[key] type:', typeof nextConfig[key]);
"
# toString in nextConfig: true
# guard passes (null return): false
# nextConfig[key] type: string
# FAIL: prototype collision bypassed guard
#   nextConfig['toString'] = Object.prototype.toString (function)
```

### After (with fix)
```bash
$ node -e "
const nextConfig = Object.create({ toString: 'inherited-prototype' });
nextConfig.agents = {};
const key = 'toString';
console.log('Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, \"' + key + '\"):', Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
console.log('guard passes (null return):', !Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, key));
"
# Object.hasOwn(nextConfig, "toString"): false
# guard passes (null return): true
# PASS: prototype collision correctly detected
#   guard returns null — safe early exit
```

### Regression test (exercises getChangedTopLevelKeys + Object.hasOwn)
```bash
$ npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  47 passed (47)
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `npx vitest run src/config/mutate.test.ts src/config/mutate.hasown.test.ts` — 47 passed (45 existing + 2 regression)
- `git diff --check` clean
- New regression tests:
  - `getChangedTopLevelKeys detects changes on own keys including prototype-named keys`
  - `Object.hasOwn check prevents prototype collision in nextConfig lookup`

target.title: fix(gateway): enforce plugin-ownership check in sessions.patch
target.body:
Closes #103077.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an in-process plugin-runtime caller could use `sessions.patch` to archive, unarchive, or otherwise mutate a session owned by a different plugin. `sessions.delete` already rejects cross-plugin cleanup, but `sessions.patch` performed the mutation with no ownership check.

## Why This Change Was Made

`sessions.patch` now checks ownership during the handler lookup and again through an `authorize` callback against the accessor snapshot used to build the projection. The lifecycle mutation lock still serializes gateway session mutations; this PR does not claim that the callback itself runs inside the SQLite write transaction.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:**
1. `sessions.patch` now propagates the authenticated plugin owner into newly created session rows, so a plugin-created row remains mutable by its creator on subsequent patches.
2. Plugin-runtime callers now fail closed on legacy ownerless rows. Rows created before plugin ownership existed have no safe plugin authority, so they are rejected rather than allowing arbitrary plugin adoption.

## User Impact

Plugin-runtime callers can no longer patch sessions created by other plugins. Their own sessions continue to work unchanged, including sessions they create through `sessions.patch`. Legacy ownerless sessions are no longer mutable by plugin-runtime callers; operators or non-plugin clients can still manage them.

## Evidence

- Regression tests in `src/gateway/server.sessions.patch-plugin-ownership.test.ts`: owned mutation allowed; foreign-owned archive and unarchive rejected; legacy ownerless row rejected; initial handler lookup miss rejected against the accessor authorization snapshot; `pluginOwnerId` stamped when patch creates a new session.
- Unit coverage in `src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` for `pluginOwnerId` stamping behavior.
- Exact head after maintainer fixup: `f8ed69034a1ebea0690b9899eb15e947d4d380ac`.
- Focused local runs on the exact head (Node 24.15.0):
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/server.sessions.patch-plugin-ownership.test.ts` → 4 passed.
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` → 81 passed.
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts` → 103 passed, 1 failed (`sessions.delete removes clean session worktrees…`; host `/usr/bin/git` is 2.27 and lacks `git init -b`; test and helper untouched by this PR, green on CI).
- `oxlint` 0 warnings / 0 errors and `oxfmt --check` clean on all 7 changed files.

## Real behavior proof

Deployed-gateway trace on the exact head: a real gateway process (worktree `dist` build, stamp head `9305961be4b`) with isolated `HOME` / `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` / `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, loopback bind, random ports, token auth, and a mock OpenAI provider (`scripts/e2e/mock-openai-server.mjs`), no real credentials. Two temporary bundled proof plugins (`sessions-patch-proof-alpha` / `-beta`) were loaded by the normal plugin loader and called `sessions.patch` through the trusted in-process plugin-runtime path (`api.runtime.gateway.request`), driven over real WebSocket RPC via `openclaw gateway call`:

- Plugin patches a session it owns → succeeds; newly created rows are stamped with the caller's `pluginOwnerId`.
- Plugin patches a session owned by another plugin → `INVALID_REQUEST` ("did not create it"); the foreign row is unchanged.
- Plugin patches a legacy ownerless row → `INVALID_REQUEST` (fail closed); a non-plugin operator client can still create and patch that row.

Full redacted transcripts, persisted SQLite before/after state, and test output are in https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/103534#issuecomment-4983631786. Remaining before merge: explicit maintainer approval of the intentional fail-closed ownerless-row compatibility boundary (P1), plus coordination with the sibling sessions.create ownership PR #103148.

target.title: fix(gateway): session workspace reveal hangs on foreground opener
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Gateway requests that open a local path could wait indefinitely when the selected platform opener stalled or synchronously owned a foreground application. This affected session workspace reveal and the shared path used by config-file open.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing shared `open-path` helper is now the canonical owner of the platform launcher lifecycle. macOS `open` and Windows PowerShell waits have a five-second deadline. Linux `xdg-open` is detached and observed for immediate startup failures for five seconds; bounded startup stderr is preserved for actionable headless-environment diagnostics, then the pipe remains drained so a foreground application can keep running without receiving `SIGPIPE` or accumulating output in the Gateway.

Both `sessions.files.reveal` and `config.openFile` remain thin callers. They retain their own validation, logging, and user-facing error wording while sharing timeout, detach, stderr-draining, and failure-propagation behavior. This also provides the canonical lifecycle requested by the review of this PR and avoids duplicating it with https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109126.

## User Impact

Revealing a session workspace or opening the active config file no longer leaves the Control UI or another Gateway client waiting forever. Missing or immediately failing launchers still produce an actionable RPC-specific error, including bounded `xdg-open` startup diagnostics, while Linux foreground applications can remain open after the request completes.

## Evidence

Real Linux process proof used the production process owner with a local executable standing in for `xdg-open`. Paths and process IDs are omitted; the output below is otherwise copied from the recorded terminal logs.

On the pre-fix main baseline, the production shared opener remained pending while the foreground-style child was alive:

target.title: fix(telegram): time out incomplete Mini App auth bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Telegram Mini App auth endpoint (`/__openclaw_tg_miniapp/auth`) had no bounded body-read lifecycle. An unauthenticated client could send an incomplete body and hold request-processing resources open.

The first version of this PR bounded the read, but real socket proof exposed a protocol bug: `readRequestBodyWithLimit` destroyed the request before the route could flush its intended HTTP 408. The client saw a silent close with zero response bytes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The route now uses the shared request-body guard, which owns the required response-before-destroy ordering for size and timeout failures. During the guarded read it also predeclares `Connection: close`, so the wire response agrees with the socket lifecycle; complete requests restore their original keep-alive state.

The regression test now uses a real `node:http` server plus a raw TCP client. It deliberately leaves a declared request body incomplete and asserts all three externally observable guarantees:

- `HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout`
- `Connection: close` with `Request body timeout`
- the client socket actually closes

## User Impact

Unauthenticated slow-body requests against the Mini App auth route are bounded by the shared 5-second pre-auth timeout. Clients receive a usable 408 response, the connection is closed, and normal complete requests retain keep-alive behavior.

## Evidence

### Focused regression test — exact head `70ed5884bb7d9b39af0e447e719732e73c8a916c`

target.title: fix(agents): prefer ordered eligible credentials in discovery map
target.body:
Fixes #110488

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where automatic/background credential discovery would pick the first same-provider auth profile in raw store insertion order, ignoring `auth.order`, OAuth-over-api_key preference, and OAuth expiry. That caused ChatGPT-mode background paths (for example automatic compaction) to fail with unusable credentials while the same session still worked through profile-aware interactive resolution.

## Why This Change Was Made

Background discovery now builds its one-credential-per-provider map through the same canonical `resolveAuthProfileOrder` ranking used for interactive profile selection, and OAuth conversion rejects expired access tokens the same way tokens already do. Discovery still does not prompt for secrets or persist resolved credentials; session-specific `authProfileOverride` plumbing for every background caller remains a follow-up if needed beyond global ordering.

Compatibility: no config/schema changes; reuses existing order/eligibility helpers. Performance: one order resolve per provider present in the store. Usability: automatic paths fail less often when a usable OAuth profile exists after an earlier api_key. Security: expired OAuth is no longer surfaced as a usable discovery credential.

## User Impact

Automatic compaction and other non-interactive model calls for a provider should select the same preferred eligible credential as interactive resolution when profiles are ordered by type or `auth.order`, instead of silently binding the first raw store entry.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (focused Vitest; path-scoped format; `git diff --check`).

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-model-discovery.auth.test.ts
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/agent-model-discovery.auth.test.ts (9 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

New cases cover: OAuth preferred over earlier same-provider api_key; `auth.order` honored; expired OAuth skipped with fallthrough to a later credential.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: provider-level discovery map no longer keeps the first raw-store credential when a preferred eligible OAuth/`auth.order` profile exists; expired OAuth is not converted as usable.
- Environment: local macOS + openclaw checkout at this PR head; focused Vitest agents lane.
- Current-main contrast: with api_key profile inserted before OAuth for the same provider, `resolveAgentCredentialMapFromStore` returned the api_key; expired OAuth with `expires > 0` still converted.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

target.title: fix(agents): Responses turns that end incomplete report zero tokens and zero cost
target.body:
Closes #100954

## What Problem This Solves

When an OpenAI/Azure Responses turn ends with `response.incomplete` — the `max_output_tokens` and
`content_filter` cases, and what Azure emits on early truncation — the agent records **zero tokens and
zero cost** for that turn. The tokens were spent and billed; the session transcript, `usage.cost` RPC and
usage bars just do not see them, so per-session accounting drifts low every time a turn is truncated.

This is the drift reported in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

`processResponsesStream` in `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts` had a terminal branch for
`response.completed` only, so `response.incomplete` matched no branch in the chain and was silently
dropped: `output.usage` was never written, `output.stopReason` never set. Unlike the package-side
processor, this one has no "stream ended before a terminal response event" guard, so nothing surfaced the
miss — the loop just ended and the turn was reported as free.

**The package side already fixed exactly this.** #109615 finalizes both terminal events through one
`finalizeResponse` (`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`), which records usage, cost and
service-tier pricing. It did not touch the agent path, and that path is live for the
`openclaw-openai-responses-transport` / `openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport` runtimes — the Azure
one being #100954's subject. So this is a sibling-parity fix: same bug, same shape of fix, the surface
#109615 left behind.

The recording lives in `src/agents/openai-responses-terminal-outcome.ts` rather than growing
`openai-responses-transport.ts`, which is a legacy file the max-lines ratchet will not let grow. Pulling
the block out drops it from **2502 to 2444 lines**, so the ratchet gets slack instead of pressure.

## Addressing the Review

Both P1 findings from the last ClawSweeper cycle are fixed in this revision.

### 1. Output backfill stays a completed-response contract

Routing `response.incomplete` into the shared terminal branch also routed it into
`backfillCompletedResponseOutput`, which had run for completed responses only. That reconstruction exists
to recover a *final answer* when item events never arrived; an incomplete turn has no final answer, so
replaying its partial output persisted truncated text the streaming path never emitted. The call is now
guarded to `response.completed`, with a regression test that fails without the guard:

```
× does not backfill message output from an incomplete Responses turn
    AssertionError: expected [ { type: 'text', …(2) } ] to deeply equal []
    +   { "text": "TRUNCATED_HALF_SENTENCE", "textSignature": "{\"v\":1,\"id\":\"msg_truncated\"}" }
```

Usage and stop-reason recording still apply to both terminal events — only the reconstruction is scoped.

### 2. One canonical terminal-usage mapper

The parallel mapper is gone. Terminal usage buckets, the stop-reason mapping and the two shared overrides
(content-filter → provider error, tool calls → `toolUse`) now live in one module,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-terminal-usage.ts`, and both `finalizeResponse` and the agent
transport call it. The duplicated `mapStopReason` and `ResponsesInputTokensDetails` in
`openai-responses-shared.ts` are deleted; the agent module drops from 103 to 68 lines and keeps only the
reasoning-token accounting the package-side `Usage` type does not carry — the thin adapter the review
asked for.

On placement: `openai-responses-shared.ts` is not reachable across the package boundary — it is not in
`packages/ai` exports, `tsconfig` paths, or the plugin-SDK resolver, and a deep import would resolve under
vitest's catch-all alias while failing `tsc` and runtime. So the mapper is its own module, re-exported
through the **existing** `internal/openai` entry point. No new subpath, no resolver or alias-test change.

### One real disagreement surfaced by merging them

The two implementations computed `totalTokens` differently: the package took the reported
`total_tokens`, the agent summed the split buckets. The canonical rule is now
`max(bucket sum, reported total)`, which keeps the provider's number while covering both directions the
old pair disagreed on — payloads that omit `total_tokens` (proxies routinely do; reporting 0 understates
the turn) and payloads whose `cached_tokens` exceeds `input_tokens`, where clamping the input bucket to 0
leaves the reported total below what the buckets actually price. Both cases are pinned by tests that fail
without the rule.

## Evidence

**The added tests fail on `origin/main` and pass here.** On main the assertions report exactly the
symptom from #100954:

```
× records Responses usage and cost when the turn ends incomplete
    AssertionError: expected +0 to deeply equal 50        <- usage.input is 0 on main
× reports content-filtered incomplete Responses turns as errors
    AssertionError: expected 'stop' to be 'error'
```

The usage test drives the real `processResponsesStream` with an Azure Responses model and an exact
`response.incomplete` event (`max_output_tokens`, populated usage with cached + cache-write tokens), then
asserts the split buckets and priced cost. Sub-cent totals round to zero at `toBeCloseTo`'s default
precision, so it also asserts `toBeGreaterThan(0)`.

**On proof shape:** #109615 pinned the identical package-side behavior with a synthetic terminal event
(`it("finalizes incomplete terminal events with usage")`,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts`) rather than a captured provider transcript.
These tests are the same shape against the agent processor. I do not have live Azure/OpenAI credentials to
attach a redacted provider transcript; if that is required before merge, a maintainer run against a real
endpoint is the remaining gap.

```
openai-responses / transport-stream / terminal-usage suites   151 passed | 0 failed (5 files)
packages/ai provider suites                                   419 passed | 0 failed (25 files)
max-lines ratchet                        OK (openai-responses-transport.ts 2502 -> 2444)
oxlint / oxfmt --check                   clean
tsgo -p tsconfig.json / test/tsconfig.json    no errors
```

## Merge Risk

Low. The `response.completed` path is unchanged in behavior — the reconstruction it depends on is now
explicitly scoped to it, and the existing transport suites cover it unchanged.

Three behaviors move, all of them the corrections above:
- `response.incomplete` records usage/cost and sets a stop reason instead of being dropped, so
  per-session totals go **up** for truncated turns — worth calling out for anyone watching usage
  dashboards.
- A content-filtered turn reports `stopReason: "error"` with `Provider incomplete_reason: content_filter`,
  matching the package side instead of a plain `length` stop.
- `totalTokens` follows the `max(bucket sum, reported total)` rule on both Responses paths, which changes
  the package-side value only for payloads that omit `total_tokens` or report one below the priced
  buckets.

This supersedes the agent-side half of #101608, which I opened before #109615 landed the package-side fix;
that PR is now conflicted and half-redundant, so I am closing it in favor of this narrower one.

AI-assisted.

target.title: perf(ui): drop typebox from Control UI startup by lazy-loading the approval page
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI initial loads carry more JavaScript than the page needs: every boot downloads and evaluates the full typebox runtime (schema builders, value checks, format validators, and its locale tables) even though only the standalone `/approve` document page uses it. That inflates cold loads, updates (new hashed assets), and remote/Tailscale sessions where the startup payload dominates time-to-interactive.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follow-up to #110472. Startup-bundle attribution through the build sourcemaps showed typebox as the single largest startup module group (130 KiB raw), reachable only via `app-host.ts`'s static import of the approval page registration — the one page not behind a lazy route. The approval page imports `approval-result-validators`, which compiles protocol schemas with typebox at module init.

The fix uses the repo's existing `OptionalCustomElement` seam (already used for the terminal panel, browser panel, and command palette): `openclaw-approval-page` now registers through a lazy module load, preloaded only when bootstrap resolves an approval document mode from the URL. The approval document template already renders a booting splash as light-DOM fallback, so the load gap is covered by design. Startup budgets are ratcheted to the new baseline (340 KiB gzip, 20 requests) per the budget script's "budget changes accompany an intentional loading decision" contract, so the win cannot silently erode.

## User Impact

Every Control UI load ships 47 KiB gzip (~250 KiB raw) less JavaScript and makes 9 fewer startup requests: startup JS drops from 369.1 KiB gzip / 22 requests to 321.8 KiB / 13 requests (−13%). Cold loads, post-update loads, and slow links benefit most. The `/approve` approval flow is unchanged: the page lazy-loads on approval URLs and renders identically.

## Evidence

- Startup attribution (sourcemap byte accounting across startup chunks): typebox 130.4 KiB raw was the largest npm group, present only via the approval-page chain; `frame-guards` and the other boot-reachable protocol modules are type-only imports and stay startup-safe.
- `node scripts/check-control-ui-performance.mjs`: startup JS 321.8 KiB gzip / 13 requests (was 369.1 KiB / 22 on main); all budgets green including the new tighter limits.
- Live verification on a real-data dev gateway: `/approve/<id>` lazy-defines and renders the approval page (correct "Approval unavailable" state for an unknown id); normal chat boot renders with no approval module in the network log.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/e2e/approval-page.e2e.test.ts` — 6 e2e tests drive a real browser against the built UI at `/approve` and pass through the lazy path.
- Focused units: `ui/src/app` (273 tests), `approval-page.test.ts` (12), `test/scripts/control-ui-performance.test.ts` — all pass.
- Full local `ui/src` sweep: 6 unrelated files fail identically on clean `main` (Node 26 experimental `localStorage` artifact; CI truth is Node 24).
- Structured autoreview (gpt-5.6-sol): clean, no findings.

target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): guard provider isConfigured probe against malformed config throws
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveConfiguredCapabilityProvider` calls the `isProviderConfigured` callback without try/catch. The callback is a direct passthrough to the provider's own `isConfigured` — if that throws (e.g. Gradium on a malformed `baseUrl`), the exception crashes capability resolution. This affects realtime transcription provider selection in voice-call and TTS talk routing.

Third sibling of #108569 and #110506 — all three fix the same throw-in-isConfigured pattern at different call sites.

## Fix

Wrap the callback invocation in try/catch. A thrown exception returns `{ ok: false, code: "provider-not-configured" }` — same result as an unconfigured provider — so other providers remain selectable.

## Evidence

### Function probe (real production function)

```
$ node --import tsx -e "import { resolveConfiguredCapabilityProvider } from ./src/plugin-sdk/provider-selection-runtime.js; ..."

=== After fix: guarded isConfigured callback ===
Result: {
  "ok": false,
  "code": "provider-not-configured",
  "configuredProviderId": "broken-provider",
  "provider": { "id": "broken-provider", "label": "Broken" }
}

Provider with broken isConfigured → { ok: false, code: "provider-not-configured" }
The exception is caught. Resolution continues to next provider.
```

target.title: fix(pairing): normalize account key in legacy allowFrom filename parsing
target.body:
Closes #110187

## What Problem This Solves

The startup-migration gate refuses to report the gateway ready when a legacy allowFrom JSON file has a non-canonical account id segment in its filename (e.g. `telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json` instead of `telegram-hy_rin_bot-allowFrom.json`). The `parseAllowFromFilename` parser cannot match it to any configured account, leaving the file unresolved. The file is never deleted, so every restart produces the same migration warning — a permanent crash loop with no in-product recovery path.

## Why This Change Was Made

`parseAllowFromFilename` compared the raw filename segment (`accountKey`) against `safeAccountKey(accountId)` without normalizing the segment first. The write path has always used `safeAccountKey` (lowercase + special-char replacement) to generate filenames, but the migration reader was not updated to apply the same normalization when parsing them. Codex review (July 17–18) on the linked issue confirmed: the parser mismatch is still present on current main, and `#108453` (default-account fallback) did not cover mixed-case or non-canonical account id spellings.

## User Impact

- Users upgrading with a legacy allowFrom file whose account segment is not in canonical `safeAccountKey` form no longer crash-loop
- The file is successfully migrated to SQLite and removed; no manual intervention needed
- Previously-working canonical filenames (e.g. `telegram-hy_rin_bot-allowFrom.json`) continue to resolve identically — `safeAccountKey` is idempotent on already-normalized inputs
- Ambiguous cases (two configured account ids that collide under `safeAccountKey`) remain unresolved with the same warning — no behavior change
- Non-canonical DEFAULT filenames (e.g. `telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json`) that do not match any configured account remain unresolved; if a configured `"default"` account exists, `safeAccountKey("DEFAULT")` = `"default"` matches it and the file migrates normally

## Evidence

**Real environment**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.18.0, branch `fix/allowfrom-accountkey-normalize-110187`, current working tree

### End-to-end `autoMigrateLegacyState` proof

This exercises the same migration entry point used by `openclaw doctor --fix` and gateway startup (`src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:586`).

**Scenario A: mixed-case HY_RIN_Bot + configured `hy_rin_bot` account → migrated, gateway can report READY**

```console
=== Scenario A: telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json with configured hy_rin_bot ===

[state-migrations] Auto-migrated legacy state:
- Migrated 1 telegram/hy_rin_bot allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state
Changes: [
  "Migrated 1 telegram/hy_rin_bot allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state"
]
Warnings: []
File still exists: false
SQLite allowFrom: {
  "hy_rin_bot": [
    "1008"
  ]
}
RESULT A: PASS
```

**Scenario B: uppercase DEFAULT, no configured "default" account → file left in place, unresolved warning blocks readiness**

```console
=== Scenario B: telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json without configured default ===

[state-migrations] Legacy state migration warnings:
- Legacy channel allowFrom channel/account is unresolved; left in place at /tmp/e2e-proof-b-xxx/.openclaw/credentials/telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json
Changes: []
Warnings: [
  "Legacy channel allowFrom channel/account is unresolved; left in place at ..."
]
File still exists: true
RESULT B: PASS (unresolved, as expected)
```

**Scenario C: uppercase DEFAULT + configured "default" account → migrated successfully**

```console
=== Scenario C: telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json WITH configured default account ===

[state-migrations] Auto-migrated legacy state:
- Migrated 1 telegram/default allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state
Changes: [
  "Migrated 1 telegram/default allowFrom entry → shared SQLite state"
]
Warnings: []
File still exists: false
SQLite allowFrom: {
  "default": [
    "1010"
  ]
}
RESULT C: PASS
```

### Scenario Matrix

Filename segment | Configured accounts | `safeAccountKey(segment)` | Expected | Result
---|---|---|---|---
`hy_rin_bot` (canonical) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `hy_rin_bot` | MATCH → `hy_rin_bot` | ✅
`HY_RIN_Bot` (mixed-case, #110187) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `hy_rin_bot` | MATCH → `hy_rin_bot` | ✅
`My_Work_Bot` (underscore-bearing mixed-case) | `["my_work_bot"]` | `my_work_bot` | MATCH → `my_work_bot` | ✅
`default` (no config) | `[]` | `default` | MATCH via fallback (literal `accountKey === "default"`) | ✅
`DEFAULT` (uppercase, no config) | `[]` | `default` | UNRESOLVED (no configured match, non-literal default) | ✅
`DEFAULT` (uppercase, with `"default"` account) | `["default"]` | `default` | MATCH → `default` (via configured-account filter) | ✅
`ops_bot` (ambiguous collision) | `["ops/bot", "ops_bot"]` | `ops_bot` | AMBIGUOUS (file kept) | ✅
`unknown` (unrelated) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | `unknown` | UNRESOLVED (file kept) | ✅
`(empty)` (pathological) | `["hy_rin_bot"]` | (throw) | SKIP (safe, no throw) | ✅

### Test output (10 channel-pairing migration tests, all pass)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts --run

 ✓ |infra| src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts (10 tests) 1921ms
     ✓ imports pairing requests and scoped allowFrom entries into SQLite
     ✓ imports a built-in channel's explicit default account without channel config
     ✓ merges with authoritative SQLite rows and keeps unreadable sources
     ✓ leaves ambiguous sanitized account filenames in place
     ✓ does not infer default accounts for external channels
     ✓ imports allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments
     ✓ imports underscore-bearing allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments
     ✓ imports uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files when a configured account matches
     ✓ leaves uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files unresolved for bundled channels
     ✓ leaves overlapping channel and account filename interpretations in place

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

### Codex Review Resolution (July 18)

Finding | Status | Change
---|---|---
Legacy filename contract unverified on current main | ✅ Confirmed | Code archaeology across 6 commits: all write paths use `safeAccountKey`; read path was missing it
Accept the historical raw account-id spelling alongside the canonical safe key | ✅ Fixed | `safeAccountKey(accountKey)` normalizes both raw and canonical spellings before comparing
Ambiguity left unresolved and explicitly reported, not guessed | ✅ Preserved | `matchingAccountIds.length > 1` → ambiguous logic unchanged
Overly broad normalization could associate a legacy allowlist file with the wrong account | ✅ Safe | `safeAccountKey` deterministic; collision → ambiguous (file kept); `removeImportedSource` only on successful match
Whether raw legacy filenames are an intentional supported input | ✅ Addressed | Not intentional, but migration code reads user disk files; not tolerating causes permanent crash loop
Whether a matching state migration already landed | ✅ Verified | Only `5e41074009` (#108453) — different root cause
Add focused regression coverage for mixed-case and underscore-bearing Telegram account IDs | ✅ Added | 3 new tests
**[P1] Keep implicit default fallback canonical** — `normalizedAccountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` broadened attribution | ✅ Fixed | Changed to `accountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` (literal comparison); removed `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard that was overly broad — now the logic first matches configured accounts via `safeAccountKey` normalization, then falls back to the implicit bundled default only when the filename suffix is the literal `"default"` and no configured account matched
**[P1] Needs real behavior proof** — no Doctor/gateway-startup evidence | ✅ Added | `autoMigrateLegacyState` end-to-end: Scenario A shows mixed-case file migrated, removed, zero warnings; Scenario B shows uppercase DEFAULT (no config) left in place with unresolved warning; Scenario C shows uppercase DEFAULT (with configured "default" account) migrated successfully
**[P1] `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard too aggressive** — blocked configured "default" account from matching `telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json` | ✅ Fixed | Removed `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard; `safeAccountKey("DEFAULT")` = `"default"` now correctly matches a configured `"default"` account via the normal filter path; implicit bundled-default fallback restricted to literal `accountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` only when no configured account matched

### Gateway startup crash-loop path (code trace)

1. `parseAllowFromFilename` returns `{ target: null, reason: "unresolved" }` — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:139`
2. `migrateLegacyChannelPairingState` pushes warning — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:271-274`
3. `channelPairing.warnings` merged into `autoMigrateLegacyState` result — `src/infra/state-migrations.doctor.ts:1265`
4. `noteStartupStateMigrationResult` pushes into `startupMigrationWarnings` — `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:413`
5. `startupMigrationWarnings.length > 0` → `throwStartupMigrationRefusal` — `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:624-630`
6. File is not deleted (unresolved → `continue`), so `hasLegacy: files.length > 0` is true on next restart — `src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts:71`

## What Changed

**`src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.ts`** (+15/-8):

- Normalize `accountKey` via `safeAccountKey` before comparing with configured account ids
- Wrap in try/catch so pathological filename segments skip safely instead of throwing
- Match configured accounts first (including `"default"` accounts that `safeAccountKey` maps from e.g. `"DEFAULT"`); then fall back to the implicit bundled-default only when `accountKey === DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` (literal) and no configured account matched
- Removed `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard that blocked configured `"default"` accounts from matching non-canonical DEFAULT filenames

**`src/infra/state-migrations.channel-pairing.test.ts`** (+83):

- Added `imports allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments` — `telegram-HY_RIN_Bot-allowFrom.json` + configured `hy_rin_bot`
- Added `imports underscore-bearing allowFrom files with mixed-case account id segments` — `telegram-My_Work_Bot-allowFrom.json` + configured `my_work_bot`
- Added `imports uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files when a configured account matches` — `telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json` + configured `"default"` account → migrated, file removed
- Added `leaves uppercase DEFAULT allowFrom files unresolved for bundled channels` — `telegram-DEFAULT-allowFrom.json` with no configured accounts → file kept in place

## What Did NOT Change

- `detectLegacyChannelPairingState` (detection logic, `accountIds` normalization via `resolveAllowFromAccountId`)
- Ambiguity detection (`matchingAccountIds.length > 1` → ambiguous, file kept in place)
- Default-account fallback for bundled channels (`CHANNEL_IDS` + literal `DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ID` check)
- `migrateLegacyChannelPairingState` callers (4 call sites in `state-migrations.doctor.ts`)
- `removeImportedSource` (only called on successful match, unchanged)
- Startup gate severity (warnings remain fatal — separate concern per #109073)
- Other legacy file types (pairing files, plugin state sidecars, session stores)

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. Normalizing `accountKey` via `safeAccountKey` for configured-account matching is the narrowest safe change. The logic now correctly handles configured `"default"` accounts matching non-canonical DEFAULT filenames (e.g. Telegram's auto-provided `"default"` account), while the implicit bundled-default fallback is restricted to the literal `"default"` suffix only when no configured account matched. Codex review confirmed across four rounds: the final approach removes the overly broad `isNonCanonicalDefault` guard and relies on the natural ordering of configured-account-match-first, implicit-fallback-second.
- **Refactor needed**: No.

## AI Assistance 🤖

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: glm-5.1
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

target.title: fix(scripts): bound conflict-marker scan reads to prevent OOM on large files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pnpm check:no-conflict-markers` previously read every candidate tracked file returned by `git grep` into memory whole via `fs.readFileSync`. A single large generated or text file that slipped through the binary heuristic could exhaust the process memory before the scan completed.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Replace the tracked-files scan with `git grep -n -z -o -I -E` so only exact conflict-marker matches are returned.
- Parse the grep output (path, line number, match) into violation records without buffering file contents.
- Parse the NUL-delimited pathname before any newline-based record splitting so tracked filenames containing newlines are reported intact.
- Keep `findConflictMarkersInFiles` for direct, small-scale use; the tracked-files path no longer reads files whole.
- `findConflictMarkersInTrackedFiles` now returns paths relative to the repository root, matching `git grep` output.

## User Impact

- Normal conflict-marker checks on source and documentation files are unchanged.
- Oversized or generated files can no longer cause an OOM during the scan because their contents are never read.
- CI and pre-commit runs remain robust against accidental large-file commits.

## Evidence

Local focused test passes:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts --run
```

Result:

```
✓ |tooling| test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts (10 tests) 633ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Terminal proof on head `b8657525ff2` against a fixture git repo containing a tracked 61 MiB file (over the previous 50 MiB scan cap) with conflict markers near the end, plus a tracked file whose name contains a newline:

```
$ du -h generated/oversized.txt
61M	generated/oversized.txt

$ node --max-old-space-size=128 scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.mjs
Found unresolved merge conflict markers:
- docs/weird
name.md:2,4,6
- generated/oversized.txt:6145,6147,6149
exit=1 (violations reported) | peak RSS 66 MB | wall clock 0.24s
```

The 61 MiB file is never read whole: the run completes in 0.24s with a 66 MB peak RSS under a 128 MB heap cap. The newline-containing path is preserved intact (`docs/weird\nname.md:2,4,6`, printed across two terminal lines because the path itself contains the newline); the previous newline-first parser silently truncated it to `name.md`. A complementary clean fixture (61 MiB, no markers) exits 0 in 0.17s with a 65 MB peak RSS.

Added regression tests covering:
- tracked files with conflict markers reported via `git grep`
- clean tracked files returning no violations
- binary tracked files skipped by `git grep -I`
- paths containing spaces and unusual characters
- tracked filenames containing newlines (NUL-delimited path parsed before record splitting)
- large files whose line numbers are reported without reading the whole file
- `main()` printing paths relative to the repository root

Rebased onto current `upstream/main` to pick up the independent `scripts/lib/sqlite-reliability-runner.ts` async/await fix that was causing `check-test-types` and `checks-node-compact-small-2` failures.

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `cd3cf83e4caeada7cba332ea0b89b4481df2e9d5` (rebased onto latest `upstream/main`).

### CLI transcript proof (exact head, redacted)

Actual `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` output at this exact HEAD (**09908298**). The `--dev` flag isolates state under `~/.openclaw-dev/`; stale plugin config warnings are redacted for brevity.

**Test 1 — Normal identity file (normal.md):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/normal-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...config warnings redacted...]
{
  "agentId": "test-agent",
  "identity": {
    "name": "CLI Proof Agent",
    "emoji": "🧪"
  },
  "workspace": "/tmp/...",
  "identityFile": "/tmp/.../normal-identity.md"
}
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 0 — identity file loaded and parsed correctly; identity values returned in JSON output.

**Test 2 — Oversized identity file (2,097,153 bytes = cap + 1):**

```text
$ node dist/index.js --dev agents set-identity --identity-file /tmp/oversized-identity.md --agent test-agent --json
[...state migration output redacted...]
Identity file /tmp/oversized-identity.md exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes
```

Result: ✅ Exit code 1 — oversized file rejected with the exact diagnostic `Identity file <path> exceeds the maximum size of 2097152 bytes`. No identity configuration was written.

The oversized-file error message is identical to what the CLI prints to stderr before exiting with code 1. This confirms the full CLI code path (command handler → bounded loader → error reporting) works correctly at this exact HEAD (**09908298**) (**09908298**).

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 386ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

### Code overview

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- `openclaw agents set-identity --identity-file` delegates to the same bounded loader and surfaces the size-limit error to the user.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` and `src/commands/agents.identity.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

target.title: fix(shared): bound ignore-file reads during workspace scans
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`addIgnoreRules` in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts` reads `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.fdignore` files with `readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size limit. A malicious or runaway ignore file in a scanned workspace can be loaded entirely into memory, causing the CLI or agent workspace scan to OOM before any rules are applied.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ignore files are line-oriented pattern lists; even large monorepos rarely exceed a few hundred KiB. A 4 MiB byte cap lets legitimate ignore files pass through while preventing an unbounded read from exhausting process memory. When a file exceeds the cap the scanner cannot know which exclusions the user asked for, so it fails closed: it conservatively excludes that directory's whole subtree from the scan. The exclusion is terminal for the directory — processing stops there so a later ignore file cannot negate it and reopen a subtree whose policy could not be parsed. Symlinked ignore files are still followed to their final regular target, preserving legacy workspace behavior.

## User Impact

- Workspace scans (`openclaw agent`, skill loading, etc.) no longer buffer arbitrarily large ignore files.
- An oversized `.gitignore` / `.ignore` / `.fdignore` now hides its subtree from discovery (fail closed) instead of dropping all of its exclusions (fail open). Workspaces with ignore files over 4 MiB will see that subtree disappear from scans until the file is trimmed below the cap.
- Normal-sized ignore files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Replaced `readFileSync` with a bounded `readRegularFileSync({ maxBytes: IGNORE_FILE_MAX_BYTES })` read in `src/shared/ignore-rules.ts`, after a direct size check that signals oversize.
- On oversize, the matcher adds `<prefix>**` and the per-directory ignore-file loop stops, so no later file can re-include the excluded subtree.
- `src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts` covers normal files, under-cap large files, oversized files, cross-file negation (oversized `.gitignore` + later `!pattern` in `.ignore`, and oversized `.fdignore` + earlier negation), and symlink chains.
- Local test run on the final head:
  ```
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/shared/ignore-rules.test.ts --run
  # 6 tests passed
  ```

## Real behavior proof (standalone, final head 01d3b33e2)

Standalone script driving the real `addIgnoreRules` / `loadSkillsFromDir` scan path in temp workspaces (no test-runner mocks):

```text
=== Normal .gitignore ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
  ignores dist/bar.js: true
  ignores src/main.ts: false
=== Large-but-under-cap .gitignore (~2.6 MB) ===
  file size: 2,600,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
=== Oversized .gitignore (~13 MB): fail-closed subtree exclusion ===
  file size: 13,000,000 bytes
  ignores ignored-file: true
  ignores anything/else.txt: true
=== Oversized .gitignore + later negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite later negation: true
  ignores secret.txt despite later negation: true
=== Oversized .fdignore + negating .ignore: exclusion stays terminal ===
  ignores ignored-file despite earlier negation: true
=== Skill discovery: oversized .gitignore + negating .ignore hides the skill ===
  skills discovered: 0
=== Symlinked .gitignore still honored ===
  ignores node_modules/foo: true
=== All standalone proof checks passed ===
```

- A 2.6 MiB ignore file is still loaded normally.
- A 13 MiB ignore file now excludes its whole subtree (fail closed), and later `!` negations in other ignore files of the same directory cannot reopen it.
- A skill directory hidden by an oversized policy is not discovered even when a later ignore file explicitly negates it.
- Symlinked `.gitignore` files are resolved to their final regular target and honored, preserving the previous workspace-scan behavior.

Agent tooling only: `scripts/pr` hosted-gate verification works through the relay-backed gh on busy SHAs without workarounds.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(linux-node): guard invalid timestamps in GeoClue output
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Linux node users requesting location could lose the entire request when GeoClue emitted an out-of-range epoch timestamp before a valid location update.

## Why This Change Was Made

The GeoClue parser now verifies that epoch milliseconds are finite and representable by JavaScript `Date` before ISO serialization. An invalid block is skipped using the parser's existing bad-block behavior; valid timestamps and the no-epoch current-time fallback are unchanged.

## User Impact

`location.get` can continue reading GeoClue output and return a later valid fix instead of failing with `RangeError: Invalid time value`.

## Evidence

Tested on Linux x86_64 with Node `v24.18.0`, based on `upstream/main` `7c1c4960c1f4aab65bb7e616eb533cdcfe68f362`.

### Real behavior proof

- Before / negative control: with the Date-valid guard temporarily reverted, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/linux-node/src/commands.test.ts -t 'keeps GeoClue running past an out-of-range timestamp'` failed in production `parseLocationOutput()` with `RangeError: Invalid time value` at `toISOString()`.
- Premise: `node --input-type=module` on this machine confirmed `new Date(1e308 * 1000).toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value`.
- After: a Node harness directly invoked exported production `createLinuxLocationCommand()`, feeding an invalid GeoClue block followed by a valid block through the command's stdout callback. Command: `node --import tsx --input-type=module < /tmp/linux-geoclue-timestamp-proof.mjs`. Observed callback state `{"invalidContinues":true,"validStops":false}` and final result `{"lat":48,"lon":16,"accuracyMeters":25,"timestamp":"2026-07-13T12:00:05.000Z","isPrecise":true,"source":"unknown"}`.
- Focused regression: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/linux-node/src/commands.test.ts` — 14 tests passed after rebasing onto the stated base.
- Static checks: direct `oxfmt --check`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed for the two changed files. Full type checking is left to PR CI because the linked worktree intentionally does not rebuild shared generated SDK declarations.
- Review: `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local` — clean, no accepted/actionable findings.

No live GeoClue service or location permission was used; this validates the supported production command/parser path with real streamed stdout bytes, including its continue/stop decisions.

target.title: fix(memory-core): guard invalid timestamps in dreaming rankings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where memory-core light dreaming could treat an invalid recall timestamp as tied with valid timestamps, preserve the wrong duplicate, and rank candidates by input order instead of recency.

## Why This Change Was Made

Dreaming ranking and owner-local duplicate merging now use the same finite-or-negative-infinity timestamp semantics already used by short-term retention. Invalid entries sort after valid entries, while recall count and existing deterministic fallbacks continue to break ties.

## User Impact

Light dreaming stages the valid, recent recall candidate when persisted recall data also contains a malformed timestamp, without changing the recall store schema or dropping entries that remain eligible through `recallDays`.

## Evidence
